skills.name: Limits from graphs, tables, and formulas
skills.description: Distinguish point values from one-sided and two-sided behavior; evaluate basic limits with justified algebra and recognize the limits of numerical evidence.
skills.theory:
A limit describes what function outputs approach as inputs approach a specified value. It is a statement about nearby inputs, not necessarily about the value at the specified input itself. The notation lim as x -> a of f(x) = L means that f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking allowed x sufficiently close to a, with x != a.

What you will learn:
Separate a function value from a limit, compare one-sided behavior, use valid algebra to evaluate finite limits, recognize infinite behavior, and explain the limitations of graphical or tabular evidence. All limits here use real inputs and outputs; infinity describes unbounded behavior rather than a real function value.

Three questions at one input:
For the function that equals x + 1 when x != 1 but is assigned f(1) = 5, ask three separate questions. What is f(1)? It is 5 by definition. What do nearby outputs approach from the left? They approach 2. What do nearby outputs approach from the right? They also approach 2. Therefore the two-sided limit is 2, even though the actual function value is 5. Leaving f(1) undefined would not change that nearby behavior.

One-sided limits:
The notation x -> a- means approach a from inputs less than a; x -> a+ means approach from inputs greater than a. The minus and plus indicate the side of the input, not the sign of the output. When both sides of a are available, a finite two-sided limit exists exactly when the two one-sided limits exist and agree. A left limit of 1 and a right limit of 3 cannot be averaged into a two-sided limit of 2.

Read the behavior, not a plotting accident:
An open circle can show a missing function value while the surrounding curve clearly approaches its height. A filled point can show the actual value without controlling the limit. Arrows, breaks, and the scale of the display matter. In an assessment, use the stated function rule or the explicit graph description rather than assuming an unlabeled screenshot resolves arbitrary precision.

Limits from tables:
A table of outputs at 0.9, 0.99, and 0.999 may suggest behavior near 1, but it samples only finitely many inputs and only one side. Other values could behave differently. A table can support a conjecture or illustrate a limit already justified from a formula; it cannot alone prove the general assertion that all sufficiently nearby allowed inputs behave as claimed. This distinction prevents numerical agreement from being mistaken for a proof.

Substitution and limit laws:
Polynomial expressions have limits found by substituting the approaching input. Sums, differences, products, and constant multiples preserve finite limits. For a quotient, divide the numerator limit by the denominator limit only when that denominator limit is nonzero. Square-root substitution is valid at allowed inputs where the root expression has the relevant limiting behavior. These rules explain why direct substitution works in ordinary cases, rather than making substitution an unconditional instruction.

A zero-over-zero result is a signal, not an answer:
For (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) as x -> 3, direct substitution gives 0/0. This is indeterminate: it does not equal zero, one, or infinity. Factor the numerator to get (x - 3)(x + 3). When x != 3, cancellation gives x + 3. Since a limit ignores the value at the single input 3, the simplified expression has the same limit, namely 6. The original function remains undefined at 3 unless a separate value is assigned.

Local equality is enough:
Two formulas need not agree everywhere to have the same limit at a. Agreement for all sufficiently nearby allowed inputs other than a is enough. This is the logical justification for cancellation in a limit argument. State the restriction under which the simplification is valid, then use the limiting behavior of the simpler expression. Do not claim that cancellation made the original denominator nonzero.

Rationalizing a root difference:
For [sqrt(x) - 2]/(x - 4) as x -> 4, multiply numerator and denominator by sqrt(x) + 2. On nearby inputs with x != 4, the quotient becomes 1/[sqrt(x) + 2]. Its denominator approaches 4, so the limit is 1/4. The conjugate removes the indeterminate form without changing the function on the punctured neighborhood where the algebra is valid.

Infinite behavior:
As x approaches zero from the right, 1/x grows beyond every positive bound; write the one-sided limit as +inf. From the left, 1/x decreases below every negative bound; write -inf. Because the directions disagree, the two-sided limit of 1/x does not exist, even as a common signed infinite limit. In contrast, 1/x^2 grows without bound from both sides, so its two-sided behavior is +inf. This is not a finite real limit and does not mean the function takes an infinite value at zero.

Endpoints and scope:
For sqrt(x) at zero, the real domain has inputs only on the right. We explicitly ask for x -> 0+ to avoid implying a nonexistent real left-side neighborhood. More advanced treatments describe limits relative to a domain; keep the requested direction clear here. In this lesson, enter DNE when no common two-sided behavior exists, and enter +inf or -inf only when the problem asks for that signed unbounded behavior.

Self-check:
Am I evaluating f(a), a one-sided limit, or a two-sided limit? Do both sides agree? Did I divide by a limiting zero without justification? Which excluded input must survive cancellation? Does my table merely suggest the answer? A sound limit argument connects nearby behavior to an exact rule or a stated theorem.

applications.description: A difference quotient describes a secant rate; its limit can describe a local rate without dividing by zero.

applications.title: Removable model defects

applications.title: Numerical computation

applications.title: Threshold behavior
applications.description: One-sided limits reveal whether a rule change is a harmless join or a genuine jump.

skills.name: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
skills.description: Check continuity with all three conditions, repair removable holes, and justify root or target-value existence using the intermediate value theorem.
skills.theory:
Continuity connects a function's value to its nearby behavior. At an interior input a, a function is continuous when f(a) exists, the finite two-sided limit as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a). These are three distinct checks. Knowing just the value, just a limit, or just one side is not enough.

What you will learn:
Test continuity at a point and across an interval, repair removable holes, distinguish jumps from unbounded behavior, handle endpoints relative to a domain, and apply the intermediate value theorem with all its hypotheses. You will separate an existence guarantee from a claim of uniqueness or an exact solution.

Apply the three checks:
If f(x) = x+1 away from x=1 but f(1)=5, the point value exists and the limit exists, but 5 is not the limit 2. The function is not continuous at 1. Redefining f(1)=2 repairs that mismatch. If no value was assigned at 1, the original function was undefined there; the repaired function is a continuous extension, not evidence that the original missing value was already present.

A removable hole:
The expression (x^2-4)/(x-2) equals x+2 for x != 2. Its nearby values approach 4. Defining the formerly missing value to be 4 produces a continuous function at that input. Any other finite assignment leaves a mismatch. The algebra determines a unique possible repair, because continuity requires equality with the existing limit.

Joining piecewise rules:
Suppose f(x) = 3x+1 for x<2 and f(x)=x+k for x>=2. The left-hand limit is 7; the right-hand limit and the actual value at 2 are 2+k. Set 2+k=7 to get k=5. This reasoning checks both the neighboring formulas and which rule defines the boundary value. If there were a separate third assignment at the boundary, it would also have to equal the common limit.

Not every break can be repaired at one point:
For x+1 below zero and x+3 above zero, the one-sided limits are 1 and 3. No choice of the single value f(0) can make the unequal sides agree. This is a jump discontinuity. Similarly, 1/x^2 becomes unbounded near zero; no finite value placed at zero can make it continuous there. A removable mismatch, a jump, and an infinite discontinuity require different diagnoses, not the same instruction to fill a dot.

Continuity on a domain:
Polynomials are continuous at every real input. A rational function is continuous wherever its original denominator is nonzero. A square-root function is continuous on its real domain in the domain-relative sense. For sqrt(x), continuity at the endpoint 0 uses the right-hand limit, because there are no negative real inputs in the domain. On a closed interval [a,b], continuity means ordinary continuity inside and the appropriate one-sided continuity at each endpoint.

Keep domain language precise:
A missing input is not a point in the function's domain. We can say 1/x is continuous on its domain, (-inf,0) U (0,inf), while also saying it cannot be used as a continuous function on [-1,1]. A cancelled factor preserves the excluded input in the original function. When a question asks for the domain on which a formula is continuous, retain that hole unless an extension is explicitly defined.

The intermediate value theorem:
Suppose f is continuous on the entire closed interval [a,b]. If a target height N lies between f(a) and f(b), then f(c)=N for at least one c in [a,b]. When N lies strictly between the endpoint values, at least one such c lies in the open interval (a,b). The theorem is about reaching every intermediate output height, not about taking every possible input or having a straight graph.

A root-existence argument:
For f(x)=x^3+x-1 on [0,1], polynomial continuity supplies the first hypothesis. The endpoint values are f(0)=-1 and f(1)=1. Zero lies strictly between them, so the theorem guarantees at least one root in (0,1). It does not say that the root is 1/2, and it does not itself establish that there is only one root. A graph may suggest a location, but the theorem supplies an existence statement even without an exact formula for the root.

Why the assumptions matter:
The function 1/x takes values -1 and 1 at the endpoints of [-1,1] but never equals zero. There is no contradiction because it is not continuous or even defined on the whole interval. Conversely, equal positive endpoint values do not establish that there is no root inside: x^2 has value 1 at both -1 and 1 but has a zero at 0. Failure of a sign-change test means that this particular existence test is inconclusive, not that roots are impossible.

Bisection as a consequence:
For a continuous function with opposite nonzero signs at interval endpoints, evaluate the midpoint. If its value is zero, a root has been found. Otherwise, keep the half whose endpoint values have opposite signs. Continuity and the theorem guarantee a root in that retained half. For x^2-6 on [2,3], the midpoint is 2.5 and its value is 0.25, while f(2)=-2. Keep [2,2.5]. Repeating the process narrows a guaranteed bracket; a midpoint is an approximation, not automatically an exact root.

Self-check:
Does the point value exist and equal a common finite limit? Have I checked the whole interval rather than only its endpoints? Is the target strictly between the endpoint heights? Does the theorem prove at least one solution, not a unique one? A continuous corner such as |x| is allowed: continuity does not require a visually smooth curve.

skills.name: Factors, multiples, primes, GCF and LCM
skills.description: Factors and multiples describe how whole numbers are built and repeated. A factor of n is a whole number that divides n with no remainder. If 4 times 9 = 36, then 4 and 9 are factors of 36, while 36 i
skills.theory:
Factors and multiples describe how whole numbers are built and repeated. A factor of n is a whole number that divides n with no remainder. If 4 times 9 = 36, then 4 and 9 are factors of 36, while 36 is a multiple of both 4 and 9. The word factor names the parts of a product; multiple names a result in a skip-counting sequence. Zero is a multiple of every whole number because 0 times k = 0, but zero is not a factor of any number because division by zero is undefined.

To list factors, test whole numbers in pairs. For 36, start at 1: 1 times 36, 2 times 18, 3 times 12, and 4 times 9. Once the smaller factor passes the square root, the pairs repeat in reverse, so the complete positive list is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. A factor-pair check is safer than guessing divisors: every claimed factor must multiply by its partner to make the target, and no pair should be counted twice. A square number such as 49 has a middle pair 7 times 7, so that factor appears once in the list even though it supplies both positions in the pair.

Prime numbers have exactly two positive factors, 1 and themselves. The number 2 is the only even prime. One is neither prime nor composite because it has only one positive factor. A composite number has at least one additional factor; 15 has 1, 3, 5, and 15. To test whether a number n is prime, try divisors up to the square root of n. If none divides evenly, no larger factor can appear without a smaller partner already found. This makes a short, reasoned test instead of a long list of guesses. Divisibility shortcuts help: a number divisible by 2 is even; one ending in 0 or 5 is divisible by 5; a number whose digit sum is divisible by 3 is divisible by 3.

Prime factorization writes a composite number as a product of primes. Factor 84 by splitting 84 = 2 times 42, then 42 = 2 times 21, and 21 = 3 times 7. Thus 84 = 2 times 2 times 3 times 7, or 2 squared times 3 times 7. The order of factors does not matter, but every factor must be prime at the end. A factor tree is a record of choices, not a different answer: splitting 84 as 6 times 14 eventually gives the same multiset of prime factors. Multiplying the primes back together checks the factorization.

The greatest common factor (GCF) of two or more numbers is the largest positive factor they share. For 24 and 36, the common factors include 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12, so the GCF is 12. A factor-list method is transparent for small numbers. A prime-factor method is efficient for larger numbers: write each number in primes, keep only primes that appear in every number, and use the smallest exponent. The GCF is useful for making equal groups as large as possible or simplifying a fraction without changing its value.

The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive number that belongs to both multiple lists. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30; multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, so the LCM is 24. With prime factors, keep every prime using the largest exponent appearing in any number. For 12 = 2 squared times 3 and 18 = 2 times 3 squared, the LCM is 2 squared times 3 squared = 36. The LCM answers repeat-together questions; the GCF answers shared-building questions. They can be linked by GCF(a,b) times LCM(a,b) = a times b for positive a and b, which is a useful check rather than a replacement for understanding.

Read the context before choosing GCF or LCM. If 48 red beads and 60 blue beads must be split into identical bags with no leftovers, the greatest possible number of bags is GCF(48,60) = 12. If a red light flashes every 8 seconds and a blue light every 12 seconds and both flash now, the next simultaneous flash is after LCM(8,12) = 24 seconds. For a factor question, ask “what equal groups fit exactly?” For a multiple question, ask “when does this repeated step land?” A number can be a factor of one target and a multiple of another; the roles depend on the sentence.

Explain your method with a product, list, or prime record. Do not call 1 prime, stop a factor tree with a composite leaf, or choose a large common factor that is not actually common. The capstone asks you to model a repeated schedule and justify why the first shared time is the least common multiple.

skills.name: Adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers
skills.description: Fractions count equal-sized parts of a chosen whole. Adding and subtracting them means combining or comparing numbers measured in the same unit. Begin with positive amounts; the signed cases later use Integer operations (MATH_ARITH_001).
skills.theory:
Fractions count equal-sized parts of a chosen whole. Adding and subtracting them means combining or comparing numbers measured in the same unit. Begin with positive amounts; the signed cases later use Integer operations (MATH_ARITH_001).

With a common denominator, the unit already matches: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. Count two sevenths and three sevenths. The denominator stays seven because adding portions does not change the size of each portion. Likewise, 6/9 - 2/9 = 4/9. Fractions may exceed one: 9/7 means one whole and two sevenths. A large numerator is not itself an error.

Unlike denominators require a common unit. To add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole, split each half into three sixths and each third into two sixths. The amounts do not change: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now count 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. The incorrect answer 2/5 is smaller than 1/2 even though a positive amount was added. More fundamentally, adding denominators invents a new unit without preserving either original fraction. Pictures must use the same-sized whole: half a small pizza and a third of a large pizza cannot be combined as fractions of one unspecified pizza.

A common multiple of the denominators supplies a common denominator. The least common multiple is efficient but not compulsory. For 1/6 + 1/4, twelfths give 2/12 + 3/12 = 5/12. Twenty-fourths give 4/24 + 6/24 = 10/24, the same value. Multiply both numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number to preserve a fraction; changing only the denominator changes its value. If one denominator divides the other, use the larger: 3/8 + 1/4 = 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8. Simplify your final fraction when useful. Equivalent exact fractions describe the same number even when written differently.

Subtraction uses the same unit rule. For 5/6 - 1/4, write 10/12 - 3/12 = 7/12. Do not subtract denominators or reverse the numerator subtraction to force a positive answer. For a missing addend, subtract the known part from the total: 2/5 + x = 7/10 gives x = 7/10 - 4/10 = 3/10. Check by adding the result back.

Mixed notation combines a whole number with a proper fraction. The number 2 3/5 means 2 + 3/5, not multiplication. Two wholes contain ten fifths, so 2 3/5 = 13/5. Conversely, 17/6 = 2 5/6 because 17 = 6 times 2 + 5. On this lesson's answer line use an improper fraction such as 13/5 rather than mixed notation unless asked for just a whole part or numerator. This avoids ambiguity while keeping an exact answer.

For mixed-number addition, convert first or add whole and fractional parts carefully. In 1 3/4 + 2 2/3, the whole parts make 3 and the fractional parts make 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12. Combine them to obtain 4 5/12, or 53/12. Do not lose the extra whole created by the fractional sum.

For mixed subtraction, exchange a whole if the first fractional part is too small. The calculation 3 1/4 - 1 2/3 becomes 2 15/12 - 1 8/12 = 1 7/12. Exchanging a whole adds twelve twelfths to the fractional part while removing one from the whole part; it does not change the starting number. Subtracting the whole parts and then reversing the fractional subtraction is invalid. Improper fractions independently check the result: 39/12 - 20/12 = 19/12.

Signed fractions follow number-line addition. For -1/2 + 3/4, start at -2/4 and move three quarter-units right, ending at 1/4. For 1/3 - (-1/6), subtracting a negative adds a positive: 2/6 + 1/6 = 1/2. A negative mixed amount, minus two and one third, means -(2+1/3) = -7/3, not -2+1/3. Parentheses make the intended sign explicit. Review signed integers first if this section is unfamiliar.

Interpret and check. A sum of positive fractions exceeds each addend. Subtracting a smaller positive amount reduces a positive starting quantity. Length, time and capacity problems need matching measurement units and a shared reference whole. Explain why the conversion preserves the amount, then explain the operation. The capstone requires equal-unit reasoning and error analysis; the number 5/6 alone does not demonstrate understanding.

skills.name: Decimal operations, powers of ten and quotient scaling
skills.description: Decimals extend place value to parts smaller than one whole. The tenths place is 1/10, the hundredths place is 1/100, and the thousandths place is 1/1000. In 4.307, the 4 means four ones, the 3 means
skills.theory:
Decimals extend place value to parts smaller than one whole. The tenths place is 1/10, the hundredths place is 1/100, and the thousandths place is 1/1000. In 4.307, the 4 means four ones, the 3 means three tenths, the 0 means no hundredths, and the 7 means seven thousandths. Trailing zeros do not change a value: 2.5 = 2.50 = 2.500. They can make alignment visible, so write equal numbers of decimal places before adding or subtracting.

Addition and subtraction combine quantities measured in the same unit. Align decimal points vertically, then add or subtract each place. For 6.40 + 2.375, write 6.400 + 2.375 = 8.775. The zeros are placeholders, not new quantity. Estimate first: 6.4+2.4 is about 8.8, so 8.775 is plausible. In a difference such as 10.000 - 3.68, write 3.680 and regroup across places. Check subtraction by adding the difference back to the smaller amount.

Multiplication by a whole number is repeated addition; multiplication by a decimal can be understood by place value and an area model. Compute 2.4×3 by first thinking 24 tenths×3 = 72 tenths = 7.2. For 0.6×0.4, six tenths times four tenths gives 24 hundredths, or 0.24. Count total decimal places in the factors as a useful placement check, then estimate the size. Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount smaller; multiplying by a number greater than 1 makes it larger.

Decimal division asks how many groups of a chosen size fit, or how much each share receives. If 8.4 litres are shared into 4 equal containers, 8.4÷4=2.1 litres each. If 8.4 metres are cut into 0.7-metre pieces, 8.4÷0.7 asks for the number of pieces, which is 12. The divisor is the unit being counted, so it cannot be zero. Division by a number between 0 and 1 can produce a larger quotient because many small groups fit in the dividend.

Powers of ten explain place shifts. Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place left: 3.47×10=34.7. Multiplying by 100 moves two places; dividing by 10 moves one place right. These are place-value changes, not a magical rule about “moving the decimal” without tracking zeros. For 0.058×1000, the 5 moves from hundredths to tens, giving 58. Dividing 5800 by 100 gives 58. If there are not enough written digits, add zeros as placeholders: 4.2÷100=0.042.

Scaling both dividend and divisor by the same nonzero power of ten leaves a quotient unchanged. This is how we make a decimal divisor a whole number: 3.6÷0.12 becomes 360÷12=30 after multiplying both numbers by 100. Scaling only the dividend changes the answer by a factor of 100; scaling only the divisor changes it in the opposite direction. Write the equality explicitly: (a×100)/(b×100)=a/b. The operation is a value-preserving rewrite, not a license to alter one part of a fraction.

Units keep decimal operations meaningful. A price of 2.40 dollars plus 0.75 dollars is 3.15 dollars; a length of 2.40 m cannot be added to 0.75 kg. In a multi-step situation, carry a unit with each intermediate value and round only when the context requires it. Keep exact decimal values while calculating so that early rounding does not accumulate error. If a display reports money to cents, explain whether the stored calculation was exact and the final display was rounded.

Use three checks: estimate the size, verify place alignment, and reverse with an inverse operation when possible. A quotient times its divisor should reconstruct the dividend, up to any stated rounding. The capstone asks you to explain why both entries are scaled when a decimal divisor is cleared and to interpret the quotient with units.
A quotient can be read in two distinct ways. If 8.4 litres are poured into 0.7-litre bottles, 8.4÷0.7 counts bottles; if 8.4 litres are shared among 0.7 groups, the context is different. The divisor is never just a number to manipulate: it names the unit or group size. When a quotient is larger than the dividend, ask whether the divisor is a positive fraction smaller than one; twelve 0.7-metre segments can fit in 8.4 metres even though 12 is larger than 8.4. This size check prevents a rule learned for whole-number divisors from becoming a false universal.

Decimal notation also supports exact fractions. Terminating decimals such as 0.125 represent 125/1000 and can be simplified to 1/8. Repeating decimals require a stated rounding policy if a display is finite. In a financial or scientific calculation, preserve a terminating exact value through the intermediate steps and round only at the reporting boundary. If an answer is a measured approximation, carry its uncertainty rather than suggesting that every displayed digit was known exactly.

skills.name: Rounding, significant figures and bounds
skills.description: Rounding replaces a value by a nearby value at a stated place. It is useful when a measurement, report, or decision does not need every recorded digit, but it changes the value. An exact value is spec
skills.theory:
Rounding replaces a value by a nearby value at a stated place. It is useful when a measurement, report, or decision does not need every recorded digit, but it changes the value. An exact value is specified without approximation in the problem’s number system, such as 3/8 or exactly 0.375 kg. A measured value may be recorded as 12.4 cm because the instrument resolves tenths; it is a report of a quantity with limited precision, not a claim that all later digits are zero.

To round to a place, keep the digits through that place and inspect the first discarded digit. If it is 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, keep the retained digit. If it is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, increase the retained digit by one. Discarded digits then become zeros in whole-number places or disappear after the decimal point. For 6,347 rounded to the nearest hundred, inspect the tens digit 4 and report 6,300. For 6,350, the tens digit is 5, so report 6,400. State the place; “6,4” is not an adequate answer to a nearest-hundred question.

Rounding can carry into a new place. Rounding 9.96 to the nearest tenth starts with retained digit 9 and a discarded hundredths digit 6. Increasing 9 tenths produces 10 tenths, which is 1 whole, so the answer is 10.0. Keep a trailing zero when it communicates the requested place. A negative number is rounded by distance to the target multiples; if signed values arise, decide using the same nearest-value idea rather than treating a minus sign as a digit.

Significant figures record meaningful digits in a measurement. Nonzero digits always count. Zeros between nonzero digits count, as in 1002 (four significant figures). Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and do not count, as in 0.00450 (three significant figures: 4, 5, and the final zero). Trailing zeros after a decimal point count, as in 2.300 (four significant figures). A whole number such as 1500 is ambiguous without notation; write 1.5×10^3 for two significant figures or 1.500×10^3 for four. Scientific notation makes the intended precision visible.

For multiplication and division, a common reporting rule is to give the result to the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs. For addition and subtraction, compare decimal places instead: align the values and report to the least precise decimal place. These rules describe a sensible measurement report; they do not make the intermediate arithmetic less exact. Keep extra guard digits during calculation, then round once at the end. Exact counted numbers, defined constants, and specified conversions do not limit significant figures in the same way as measured inputs.

Bounds make an approximation informative. If a value x rounds to 48.4 to the nearest tenth, then 48.35 ≤ x < 48.45. The lower endpoint is included because 48.35 is exactly halfway and rounds up under the usual half-up convention; the upper endpoint is excluded because 48.45 would round to 48.5. For rounding to the nearest whole number n, the interval is [n−0.5,n+0.5). If a displayed value is truncated rather than rounded, its bounds differ: 48.4 truncated to one decimal means 48.4 ≤ x < 48.5.

Use a symbol or inequality for uncertainty instead of inventing digits. A mass reported as 2.30 g to the nearest hundredth lies from 2.295 g up to but not including 2.305 g. A calculation using bounds can estimate a range for an area or cost, but the result’s precision should not imply more knowledge than the inputs provide. Do not confuse accuracy (closeness to a true value) with precision (repeatable detail or resolution); rounding changes the reported precision, while calibration affects accuracy.

Before rounding, identify the target place or number of significant figures. Mark the last kept digit, inspect the next digit, and perform any carry. Afterward, check that the notation still communicates the requested precision and that the result is close to the original. The capstone asks you to give a rounded measurement and its half-open bounds, and to explain why the upper endpoint is excluded.
Rounding is a communication decision as well as a calculation. A bus timetable may round a duration to the nearest minute, while a laboratory report may retain hundredths because the instrument supports them. The same underlying value can therefore have several honest displays, provided each display states its place or significant-figure rule. When comparing rounded values, remember that two displays can overlap in their possible true intervals; a visible difference does not always prove the underlying values differ.

A bound is an interval statement, so endpoint symbols carry information. For nearest-tenth half-up rounding, the lower midpoint belongs to the displayed bin and the upper midpoint belongs to the next bin. If a problem uses a different tie rule, such as ties-to-even, state that rule before changing the endpoint. Bounds are also useful in later calculations: adding lower bounds gives a lower bound for a sum when all quantities are nonnegative, while multiplying bounds requires attention to signs. Keep the simple one-value interval separate from those later interval operations.

skills.name: Ratios, unit rates and proportional sharing
skills.description: A ratio compares quantities by division or by a colon notation such as 3:5. The order matters: 3 red beads to 5 blue beads is not the same statement as 5 red to 3 blue. A ratio can compare parts of on
skills.theory:
A ratio compares quantities by division or by a colon notation such as 3:5. The order matters: 3 red beads to 5 blue beads is not the same statement as 5 red to 3 blue. A ratio can compare parts of one collection or two different units, but label the quantities so the comparison is interpretable. The ratio 3:5 means that for every 3 units of the first quantity there are 5 units of the second; it does not by itself say the collection has only 8 units.

Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both parts by the same nonzero factor. 3:5, 6:10, and 15:25 describe the same relationship. To simplify 18:30, divide both entries by their GCF, 6, giving 3:5. Dividing only one side destroys equivalence. A ratio table keeps the paired values in columns, while a double number line places corresponding values at the same scaled positions. Both representations make the “same multiplier” visible and help detect a reversed or uneven scaling.

A unit rate is a rate for one unit of the reference quantity. If 240 km takes 4 hours, the unit rate is 240÷4 = 60 km per hour. The denominator tells what “per one” means. Cost per item, litres per minute, and pages per day are all unit rates; swapping numerator and denominator changes the question. A rate can be used forward by multiplying by the number of reference units, or backward by dividing a total by the unit rate. Carry units through every step so that 60 km/h is not mistaken for 60 hours/km.

Proportional situations have a constant ratio or constant unit rate. If 3 notebooks cost $6, then 1 notebook costs $2 and 8 notebooks cost $16, assuming the same price rule. The relationship can be represented by a table, a double number line, an equation y=kx, or a graph through the origin. A fixed delivery fee breaks direct proportionality: two items may cost more than twice the cost of one if the fee is charged once. Check the context before extending a ratio.

To share a total in a ratio, add the ratio parts to find the number of equal shares. For 3:5 and a total of 64, there are 8 parts, so one part is 64÷8=8. The first amount is 3×8=24 and the second is 5×8=40. Check 24+40=64 and 24:40 simplifies back to 3:5. This is different from taking 3/5 of the total: the first share is 3/(3+5) of the total because the total includes both groups.

Percent, fraction, and ratio language can connect, but do not silently switch reference bases. A ratio of 1:4 means 1 out of 5 total parts if the two parts exhaust a whole, which is 20%, not 25%. A ratio of boys to girls 1:4 does not mean boys are 25% of all pupils unless those are the only two groups; it means one boy for every four girls. State whether a fraction is part-to-whole or part-to-part.

Scale drawings and maps use ratios with units that may differ. A map scale 1 cm:5 km means 3 cm represents 15 km. Convert units before comparing rates, and use a proportion with matched columns. A good table repeats the same multiplier down both columns. If one known pair is 4 tickets for $18, then 10 tickets at the same unit price cost $45; if the context has bulk discounts, that inference needs qualification.

Read ratio questions in order: name the two quantities, decide whether the comparison is part-to-part or a rate, simplify or scale both entries, and verify units and totals. The capstone asks you to share a fixed total fairly according to a ratio and justify the part-to-whole calculation.
A ratio table is a claim about correspondence, not merely a convenient arrangement of numbers. If 4 tickets cost 18 dollars and the relationship is proportional, every row has cost/tickets=4.50 dollars per ticket. A row such as 10 tickets for 40 dollars would signal a changed price rule, a discount, or an error. State which assumption you are using before extrapolating.

Rates can be converted without changing the underlying relationship. For 60 km/h, multiplying numerator and denominator by 1000 and 3600 gives 1,000 m/3,600 s, or 16 2/3 m/s. The number changes because the reference units change, but the physical motion is the same. In a share, the ratio parts are dimensionless counts; the total carries dollars, grams, or people, so the value of one part inherits the total unit. These distinctions keep ratio arithmetic connected to the situation.

skills.name: Percentages, reverse percentages and percentage points
skills.description: A percent is a rate per hundred. The symbol % means divide by 100, so 20% = 20/100 = 0.20 = 1/5. A percentage can describe a part of a reference base, a change from an earlier value, or a comparison b
skills.theory:
A percent is a rate per hundred. The symbol % means divide by 100, so 20% = 20/100 = 0.20 = 1/5. A percentage can describe a part of a reference base, a change from an earlier value, or a comparison between two groups. Always name the base: 20% of 80 is 16, while 20% of 200 is 40. The same percent does not mean the same number when the base changes.

To find p% of an amount A, multiply A by p/100. For 15% of 60, use 0.15×60=9. To find what percent a part B is of a base A, divide B by A and multiply by 100: 18 is 30% of 60 because 18/60=0.30. A percent increase from old value O to new value N is (N−O)/O×100%; the old value is the reference base. A decrease uses the same formula with the signed change or with O−N as a positive decrease.

Percent change is not the same as percentage points. If a survey share moves from 40% to 55%, the increase is 15 percentage points because 55−40=15. Relative percent change is 15/40×100%=37.5%, because the original 40% is the base. Say which one you mean. A move from 0.40 to 0.55 can be described as +0.15 in proportion units, +15 percentage points, or a 37.5% relative increase.

A forward percentage change uses a multiplier. Increasing by r% multiplies the old amount by 1+r/100; decreasing by r% multiplies it by 1−r/100. An 80% result after a 20% decrease came from 100 because 100×0.80=80. Two successive changes multiply their factors: a 20% increase then a 20% decrease gives 1.20×0.80=0.96, a net 4% decrease. The percentages act on different intermediate bases, so “up 20 then down 20” does not cancel.

Reverse percentages undo the multiplier. If a final value F is after an r% increase, original O=F/(1+r/100). If F is after an r% decrease, O=F/(1−r/100). Do not subtract r% of the final value when reversing a change; the final value is not the original reference base. For a 20% discount, a sale price of $80 means O=$80/0.80=$100. The check is to apply the stated change forward and recover $80.

Percentage points are especially useful for rates, probabilities, and survey shares. A tax rate moving from 5% to 6% rises 1 percentage point, but its relative increase is 20% because 1/5=0.20. A percentage point is an absolute difference between percentages; percent change is a ratio of a difference to a base. Keep the percent sign attached to rates and use a separate unit such as “points” when comparing them.

Rounding can enter at the final display, but keep the unrounded multiplier while calculating. A discount of 12.5% is exactly one eighth, so multiplying by 0.875 may be clearer than subtracting a rounded dollar amount. In a context, identify whether the question asks for the percent, the percentage amount, the final value, or the original value. Label the reference base and check by reversing the operation. The capstone asks you to recover an original price from a reduction and to explain why the final price cannot be used as the base for a simple subtraction.
A percentage amount and a percentage rate should be kept separate. Saying “the discount is 20%” gives a rate; saying “the discount is $16” gives an amount for a particular base. To compute the amount, multiply the rate by the base. To compare two discounts, compare both their rates and the bases they act on. A $16 discount could be 20% of $80 or 8% of $200, so the dollar amount alone does not identify the percentage.

Repeated changes are easiest to audit by naming each base. Start with O, apply the first multiplier to get an intermediate value, then apply the second multiplier to that intermediate value. If a quantity decreases by 10% three times, the multiplier is 0.9³, not 0.7; “30% total” would be a different policy. Reverse each multiplier in reverse order if you need to recover an original after several stages. For a final rate, also distinguish a percentage-point change from a percent change in the rate itself, especially when the old rate is small.

skills.name: Measurement, unit conversions and elapsed time
skills.description: Measurement attaches a number to a unit so that a length, mass, time, or capacity can be interpreted. A bare 5 is incomplete when a question asks for distance or duration: 5 m, 5 kg, and 5 min are dif
skills.theory:
Measurement attaches a number to a unit so that a length, mass, time, or capacity can be interpreted. A bare 5 is incomplete when a question asks for distance or duration: 5 m, 5 kg, and 5 min are different quantities. Choose a unit that suits the scale, record the given unit, and convert with an equality before calculating. The equality 1 m = 100 cm is a relationship between units, not a statement that the physical length changed.

For a single dimension, conversion factors multiply by 1 in value. To convert 2.4 m to centimetres, use 2.4 m×(100 cm/1 m)=240 cm; the metres cancel. To convert 3500 g to kilograms, use 3500 g×(1 kg/1000 g)=3.5 kg. Larger units have more physical size, so the numerical count usually decreases when moving from small units to large units. Write the units through the calculation instead of relying only on a decimal-point memory trick.

Area and volume scale in powers of the linear conversion. Since 1 m=100 cm, a square metre is 1 m²=(100 cm)²=10,000 cm². A cubic metre is 1 m³=(100 cm)³=1,000,000 cm³. Converting 25,000 cm² to m² means divide by 10,000, giving 2.5 m²; dividing by 100 would be a one-dimensional conversion and would be wrong. For a box, 1 L=1000 cm³, so 2500 cm³=2.5 L. Count the dimension: length uses the factor once, area twice, and volume three times.

Perimeter adds lengths around a boundary; area measures a surface; volume measures occupied space. A rectangle 3 m by 2 m has perimeter 10 m and area 6 m². The units themselves help catch a category error: m cannot equal m², and adding 3 m to 2 m² is not meaningful. If dimensions are given in different units, convert them first, then apply the formula. A scale drawing may require converting the final area or volume with the correct power.

Elapsed time is a difference between instants, but clock notation is not ordinary decimal notation. From 09:35 to 11:10, count 25 minutes to 10:00 and 70 minutes from 10:00 to 11:10, for 95 minutes or 1 h 35 min. Borrow one hour as 60 minutes, not as 100. If a duration crosses midnight, split at 24:00. For a schedule, distinguish start time, end time, and duration; a break may need to be removed from the total.

Unit rates connect measurement to time or quantity: 180 km in 3 h is 60 km/h, while 3 h for 180 km is 1/60 h/km. Converting before dividing avoids hidden factors. For speed, distance = speed×time only when units are compatible; 90 km/h for 30 minutes uses 0.5 h and gives 45 km. For medication, recipes, or engineering, keep units attached so a conversion is visible and reversible.

Significant figures and rounding belong at the reporting stage. Keep exact conversion factors such as 100 cm per metre and 60 seconds per minute, then round a measured result according to the stated precision. A count of 60 seconds in a minute is a defined relationship; a stopwatch reading may be approximate. Check plausibility: converting metres to centimetres should increase the number by 100, while converting square metres to square centimetres should increase it by 10,000.

A reliable workflow is: name the quantity and unit, write a conversion equality, cancel units, calculate, and state the final unit. For time, draw a timeline or split at a convenient hour. The capstone combines mixed length units and area, asking you to square the conversion factor rather than reuse a one-dimensional factor.
Dimensional analysis is a cancellation argument. Write a conversion factor so the unit you do not want appears once in the numerator and once in the denominator. If a conversion factor is squared, both copies of the length unit are transformed: (1 m)²=(100 cm)². Do not convert a finished area by 100 and call the result square centimetres; the missing factor of 100 is a dimensional error, not a rounding issue.

Elapsed-time problems often combine a duration with a clock time. Add 95 minutes to 09:35 by adding 25 minutes to reach 10:00, then 70 more to reach 11:10. For a schedule with a break, calculate the gross interval first and subtract the break duration in minutes. For speeds, convert every time to hours or every distance to a matching unit before multiplying. A result such as 45 km is plausible for 90 km/h over half an hour; 2,700 km would reveal that minutes were treated as hours.

skills.name: Scientific notation arithmetic and orders of magnitude
skills.description: Scientific notation writes a nonzero number as a×10^n, where 1≤|a|<10 and n is an integer. The coefficient a carries the meaningful leading digits; the exponent n records how far the decimal point is
skills.theory:
Scientific notation writes a nonzero number as a×10^n, where 1≤|a|<10 and n is an integer. The coefficient a carries the meaningful leading digits; the exponent n records how far the decimal point is from the displayed coefficient. For example, 4,700,000 = 4.7×10^6 and 0.000047 = 4.7×10^-5. The exponent is a count of place shifts, not a measurement unit and not the number of zeros in every written form.

To convert a large number to scientific notation, move the decimal point left until one nonzero digit remains before it. Count left moves as a positive exponent. For a small positive number, move right and use a negative exponent. Restore the ordinary number by reversing the shifts. A zero has no normalized scientific notation because it has no first nonzero digit; write 0 separately. Negative values keep the negative sign in the coefficient, such as −3.2×10^4.

Multiplication uses the product of coefficients and addition of exponents: (a×10^m)(b×10^n)=(ab)×10^(m+n). If |ab| is outside [1,10), normalize by shifting its decimal and adjusting the exponent. Example: (3×10^4)(2×10^3)=6×10^7. For 8×10^5 times 4×10^2, the raw coefficient 32 becomes 3.2 and the exponent 7 becomes 8, giving 3.2×10^8. Keep the coefficient and power parts separate until the final normalization.

Division divides coefficients and subtracts exponents: (a×10^m)/(b×10^n)=(a/b)×10^(m−n), with b nonzero. If a/b is less than 1, normalize by moving the decimal right and reducing the exponent. For (6×10^7)/(2×10^3), the coefficient quotient is 3 and exponent difference is 4, so the result is 3×10^4. Check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.

Addition and subtraction require matching powers of ten first. You may rewrite 2.4×10^6 as 24×10^5, or rewrite 7×10^5 as 0.7×10^6. Then combine coefficients with the same power: 2.4×10^6 + 0.7×10^6 = 3.1×10^6. Adding coefficients while ignoring different exponents is a common error: 2×10^6 + 3×10^4 is not 5×10^10. For widely separated exponents, an estimate may show that the smaller term changes only later digits, but keep it when an exact sum is requested.

Orders of magnitude compare powers of ten. A value near 7×10^6 has order 10^6; a value 7×10^−6 has order 10^−6. If “nearest order” is requested, compare the coefficient to √10≈3.16: 7×10^6 is closer on a logarithmic scale to 10^7 than 10^6, while 2×10^6 is closer to 10^6. In elementary comparisons, the exponent gives the main scale, then the coefficient breaks ties. State whether you mean exponent-based scale or nearest power, because those are different conventions.

Scientific notation is especially helpful for unit conversions, astronomy, cells, computing storage, and rates with extreme scales. Keep units beside the coefficient and do not let a prefix such as micro- silently alter the exponent. Significant figures live in the coefficient: 4.70×10^3 has three significant figures, while 4.7×10^3 has two. Round only after arithmetic and normalize again after rounding. The capstone asks you to multiply two quantities with opposite exponents, normalize the coefficient, and explain why the exponents add.
The exponent rules are consequences of place-value multiplication. Ten to the fourth times ten to the third is ten to the seventh because four place shifts followed by three more shifts make seven shifts. Division reverses those shifts, so a negative exponent naturally represents a reciprocal: 10^-3=1/1000. This interpretation helps when an answer is written in ordinary notation and prevents sign mistakes in exponent subtraction.

Normalization is not optional decoration. A coefficient of 32 violates the convention 1≤|a|<10, so either shift its decimal point or leave it explicitly unnormalized and label it as an intermediate. After addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, check the coefficient range and adjust the exponent exactly once. For addition with distant powers, align exponents before combining; for example, 2.0×10^8+3.0×10^5=2.003×10^8, not 5.0×10^13. The exponent indicates scale while the coefficient preserves the leading detail.

Orders of magnitude are a comparison tool, not an automatic rounding answer. Two values with exponents differing by six are separated by a million before coefficient effects. When coefficients are close to a threshold such as 3.16 for nearest-power conventions, state the convention and compare the values rather than relying on the exponent alone. Units remain attached: 4×10^3 m and 4×10^3 kg have the same numerical scale but describe different quantities. Scientific notation makes that distinction visible when the unit is written beside the number.

skills.name: Direct and inverse proportion
skills.description: A proportional model describes a particular relationship between quantities. You must identify the quantities, their units, and the conditions under which the model makes sense. A table or graph can suggest a model; an unexplained pattern in a few measurements is not a proof that the model will work everywhere.
skills.theory:
A proportional model describes a particular relationship between quantities. You must identify the quantities, their units, and the conditions under which the model makes sense. A table or graph can suggest a model; an unexplained pattern in a few measurements is not a proof that the model will work everywhere.

Direct proportion means y = kx with one fixed constant k on the stated domain. For x not zero, y/x = k. If each metre of identical ribbon costs 3 currency units and there is no extra fee, 2 metres costs 6 and 5 metres costs 15. Doubling the length doubles the cost. The unit rate is 3 currency units per metre. Zero metres costs zero, so the complete mathematical line goes through the origin. In a context, only nonnegative lengths may make sense even though the formula can accept negative inputs.

Find k by dividing an output by its matching nonzero input, not by dividing two outputs from different rows. If y = 18 when x = 6, then k = 18/6 = 3. Use y = 3x to find another output, or divide y by 3 to recover an input. A ratio table scales both quantities by the same factor. The factor may be a fraction: halving a quantity halves its directly proportional partner. Matching units matters: convert minutes to hours before comparing rates quoted per hour.

A straight line is not automatically direct proportion. A delivery charge y = 3x + 5 is linear, but the fixed fee makes y/x depend on x. For x = 1 the ratio is 8; for x = 2 it is 11/2. The graph does not pass through the origin, and doubling x does not double y. A constant difference between consecutive outputs shows a constant slope when inputs have equal steps; it does not by itself show a constant output-to-input ratio. In contrast, for y = 3x, both the slope and the direct-proportion test agree.

Inverse proportion means y = k/x with a fixed nonzero k on a domain excluding x = 0. The product xy = k remains fixed. If a fixed 24-litre supply is shared equally among x identical containers, each receives y = 24/x litres. Twice as many containers means half as much in each, and three times as many means one third as much. The constant has units of the product: in this example container-count times litres per container gives the fixed number of litres. With x as a positive count, only positive integer inputs are physically possible even if a smooth curve helps show the pattern.

Find an inverse constant by multiplying a matched input and output. If y = 8 when x = 3, then k = 24; y = 24/x gives y = 4 at x = 6. To find x from y, solve xy = k, so x = k/y when y is nonzero. Do not use y/x here: that ratio changes. For positive k and positive inputs, the graph curves down as x grows. It approaches the axes without meeting them. The point x = 0 is excluded, not a hidden value on the vertical axis, and the curve must not be drawn across that gap.

Not every decreasing relationship is inverse proportion. The rule y = 10 - x decreases but its product xy is not fixed: at x = 2 the product is 16, while at x = 3 it is 21. Likewise, not every increasing relationship is direct: y = x squared has ratios x, not one constant. Check the invariant the definition requires. For direct proportion test y/x wherever x is nonzero and include the origin when the domain includes zero. For inverse proportion test xy and exclude zero from the input domain. A single matching pair cannot distinguish the models; both can be made to pass through one nonzero point.

Real situations need assumptions. More workers may shorten a job in inverse proportion only when the amount of work is fixed, workers have equal constant productivity, and they can work independently without delays. Doubling workers need not halve travel time or a task with a single shared machine. A constant-speed journey has distance directly proportional to time, whereas time is inversely proportional to speed for a fixed distance. Naming which quantity is fixed prevents these statements from being confused.

Representations should tell the same story. Use a table to test the ratio or product, an equation to calculate exact values, and a graph to see shape and domain. Axis scales may differ, so the angle a line seems to make on screen is not its numerical slope. The generated graphs in this lesson are drawn from the stated formula and parameters, not from a hidden answer. Explain why you selected a model, state its restrictions, and verify a result in the original relation. The reviewed capstone compares direct proportion, a line with an intercept and inverse proportion; selecting a familiar formula without justification is insufficient.

skills.name: Angle relationships and parallel lines
skills.description: Name angles precisely, use angle sums, and justify parallel-line conclusions from a transversal.
skills.theory:
An angle is formed by two rays with a common endpoint. The endpoint is the vertex, and the rays are its sides. The notation angle ABC names the vertex in the middle: B is the vertex, while A and C lie on the two sides. A segment has two endpoints and stops at both ends; a ray has one endpoint and continues forever in one direction; a line continues in both directions. Naming the objects prevents a common error: an angle is not the same thing as either one of its boundary segments.

Angles are measured by the amount of turn between their sides. A right angle is 90 degrees, an acute angle is between 0 and 90 degrees, an obtuse angle is between 90 and 180 degrees, and a straight angle is 180 degrees. A full turn around a point is 360 degrees. Adjacent angles share a vertex and one side without overlapping interiors. A linear pair is an adjacent pair whose other sides are opposite rays, so its measures add to 180 degrees. Vertical angles are opposite angles made by two intersecting lines; they have equal measure because each is supplementary to the same neighboring angle.

Around a point, all the small angles add to 360 degrees. This fact works whether the rays make a neat compass shape or a crowded, rotated sketch. A straight line through a point contributes 180 degrees, so the angles on one side of that line add to 180 degrees. Always identify the complete turn or straight path before subtracting. A diagram may be rotated or may not be drawn to scale; stated marks and measures control the reasoning.

Parallel lines are coplanar lines that never meet, even when extended. The symbol p || q records a hypothesis, not a visual impression. A transversal is a line or segment that crosses two other lines at distinct points. At each crossing, four angles are made. If p || q, corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, alternate exterior angles are equal, and same-side interior (co-interior) angles are supplementary. These rules are relationships between angle positions, not between arbitrary labels. Trace the transversal and compare which side of it and which region between the two lines each angle occupies.

The converse matters. If a transversal cuts two lines and a pair of corresponding angles is equal, or a pair of alternate interior angles is equal, then the two lines are parallel. If same-side interior angles add to 180 degrees, the lines are parallel. The converse cannot be used without a qualifying angle relationship. Two angles can happen to have equal measures in an unrelated drawing, and a single equal pair at one intersection does not establish parallelism unless the pair is positioned as a converse theorem requires.

A dependable solving routine is: (1) copy the givens, including p || q or a right-angle mark; (2) name the angle relationship; (3) write an equation using equality or a 180/360 degree sum; (4) solve and check that the result has the expected size. For a missing angle x next to 68 degrees on a straight line, x + 68 = 180, so x = 112 degrees. For a vertical angle opposite 68 degrees, x = 68 degrees. For three angles around a point, x + 95 + 125 = 360, so x = 140 degrees.

Transversal examples are easiest when you first find a matching angle and then use a local fact if needed. Suppose corresponding angles are 74 degrees; every corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior partner is 74 degrees, while each adjacent supplement is 106 degrees. The entire pattern has only two measures, 74 and 106. This does not mean every angle in every parallel-line picture is equal: the supplementary family remains different unless the transversal is perpendicular to the parallel lines.

Converse reasoning also explains why parallel symbols must be explicit. A picture with two lines that look horizontal can be a perspective drawing or a deliberately misleading nonexample. Use the stated p || q, a marked equal pair in the correct positions, or a stated supplementary pair. A ray can be a transversal if it intersects both lines, but it has an endpoint; do not silently call it a full line. A segment may cross two lines in a finite diagram, but the theorem only concerns the portion and the lines it meets.

In applications, angle relationships describe roof trusses, road intersections, tile patterns, camera sight lines, and map grids. The units are degrees, not centimetres or square units. Keep exact integer sums when possible, and use a calculator only when a non-integer angle is explicitly given. A correct explanation identifies the geometric reason, such as “alternate interior angles are equal because p || q,” rather than saying merely that the picture looks right.

Self-check: Did I put the vertex in the middle of a three-letter name? Are the sides rays or segments as stated? Did I distinguish vertical from adjacent angles? Did I use the parallel hypothesis before applying a transversal theorem? If I used a converse, did I verify the angle positions? Do all angles at a point total 360 degrees and all straight-line pairs total 180 degrees?

examples.prompt: Name the vertex and sides of angle ABC.
examples.solution: B is the vertex; rays BA and BC are the sides.
examples.explanation: The middle letter names the common endpoint. The sides are rays starting at B and passing through A and C.

examples.prompt: Two lines intersect. One angle is 68 degrees. Find its vertical angle and each adjacent angle.
examples.solution: Vertical angle 68 degrees; each adjacent angle 112 degrees.
examples.explanation: Vertical angles are equal. Each adjacent linear-pair angle is 180 - 68 = 112 degrees.

examples.prompt: Three rays around point O make angles 95 degrees, 125 degrees, and x. Find x.
examples.explanation: Angles around a point total 360 degrees, so x = 360 - 95 - 125 = 140 degrees.

examples.prompt: A straight angle is split into 47 degrees and x. Find x.
examples.explanation: A straight angle is 180 degrees, so x + 47 = 180.

examples.prompt: Lines p and q are parallel. A transversal makes a 74 degree angle in the upper-left position at p. Find the corresponding angle at q.
examples.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.

examples.prompt: In parallel lines p || q, one interior angle is 112 degrees. Find its alternate interior partner and its same-side interior partner.
examples.solution: Alternate interior 112 degrees; same-side interior 68 degrees.
examples.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal, while co-interior angles sum to 180 degrees.

examples.prompt: Two lines cut by a transversal have alternate interior angles both equal to 63 degrees. What conclusion is justified?
examples.explanation: Equal alternate interior angles establish parallelism by the converse theorem.

examples.prompt: A transversal crosses two lines, and same-side interior angles measure 121 degrees and 59 degrees. What conclusion is justified?
examples.explanation: 121 + 59 = 180 degrees, so the supplementary co-interior converse applies.

examples.prompt: A diagram labels a ray AB and a segment CD. Which object has exactly one endpoint?
examples.explanation: A ray starts at A and continues through B; a segment has two endpoints.

examples.prompt: One angle at a parallel-line intersection is 38 degrees. List the only two measures appearing among all eight angles.
examples.explanation: Vertical, corresponding, and alternate angles copy 38 degrees; adjacent angles are its supplement, 142 degrees.

skills.name: Triangles, quadrilaterals, and polygons
skills.description: Classify polygons, use interior and exterior angle sums, and justify triangle and quadrilateral properties.
skills.theory:
A polygon is a simple closed figure made from straight line segments. “Simple” means its sides do not cross except at shared endpoints. The sides meet at vertices, and the angles inside are interior angles. A polygon with n sides has n vertices and n interior angles. A three-sided polygon is a triangle; four sides make a quadrilateral; five, six, and seven sides make pentagons, hexagons, and heptagons. The name counts sides, even when the figure is rotated or drawn with unequal-looking lengths.

Convexity is a useful first classification. A convex polygon has every interior angle less than 180 degrees and every diagonal inside the figure. A concave polygon has at least one reflex interior angle greater than 180 degrees, and some diagonal leaves the figure. A star-like self-intersecting outline is not a simple polygon for the ordinary interior-sum formulas. Do not infer convexity from a small picture; inspect the angles and crossings described by the problem.

The interior-angle sum of an n-gon is (n - 2) * 180 degrees. The reason is triangulation: choose one vertex of a convex polygon and draw diagonals to all non-neighboring vertices. This creates n - 2 triangles, each contributing 180 degrees. A quadrilateral therefore has 2 * 180 = 360 degrees, a pentagon 540 degrees, and a hexagon 720 degrees. The same sum remains valid for a simple concave polygon if its reflex angle is counted as an interior angle greater than 180 degrees; the triangulation or an equivalent angle argument must be interpreted carefully.

For a regular polygon, all sides and all interior angles are equal. Divide the interior sum by n to get one interior angle: ((n - 2) * 180) / n. An exterior angle is formed by extending one side and using the adjacent outside turn. For a convex polygon, the exterior angles, taken one at each vertex in the same direction, sum to 360 degrees. A regular n-gon therefore has exterior angle 360/n degrees, and its interior angle is 180 - 360/n degrees. “Exterior angle” must be chosen consistently; mixing an interior reflex angle with a small outside turn creates a false equation.

Triangle facts give a strong hierarchy. Every triangle has three sides and interior sum 180 degrees. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60-degree angles; it is also isosceles because it has at least two equal sides. An isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides and equal opposite base angles. A scalene triangle has no equal sides. A right triangle has one 90-degree angle; an acute triangle has all angles less than 90 degrees; an obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90 degrees. These classifications overlap: an isosceles triangle can be right, acute, or obtuse, while an equilateral triangle is acute.

The triangle inequality is necessary for three lengths to form a nondegenerate triangle: the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third. It is enough to check the two shorter sides against the longest. Lengths 4, 7, and 10 work because 4 + 7 > 10; lengths 3, 5, and 8 fail because 3 + 5 = 8 and would flatten into a segment. The largest angle lies opposite the longest side, and equal sides face equal angles. These comparisons are valid even when the sketch is rotated.

Quadrilateral properties also form a hierarchy. Under the explicit convention used here, a trapezoid is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, so it is a trapezoid under this inclusive convention. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, hence also a parallelogram and a trapezoid. A kite has two distinct pairs of adjacent equal sides; it need not be a parallelogram. State the convention when a classification question uses “trapezoid,” because some texts require exactly one pair.

A rotated figure keeps every side length, angle measure, parallel relation, and classification. A square tilted 30 degrees is still a square; a trapezoid turned upside down still has its same pair of parallel bases. Use marks and stated facts, not screen orientation. For a missing angle, first select the most specific property available, then use a sum. A rectangle gives four 90-degree angles immediately, while a general quadrilateral only gives a 360-degree total.

Self-check: Did I count sides rather than apparent corners? Is the figure simple and convex or concave? Did I use (n - 2) * 180 for an interior sum and 360 for a complete exterior turn? Did I distinguish “at least one pair” from “exactly one pair” of parallel sides? Did I apply the triangle inequality strictly, and did rotation change only the page orientation?

skills.name: Perimeter, area, and composite plane figures
skills.description: Calculate perimeter and area, find missing dimensions, and decompose or subtract composite figures with correct units.
skills.theory:
Perimeter measures the total distance around a two-dimensional boundary. Area measures the amount of surface inside that boundary. They use different units: a rectangle with side lengths in metres has perimeter in metres and area in square metres. A drawing can have a large perimeter and small area or a small perimeter and large area, so never swap the formulas. Perimeter follows the outside edge only; internal partition lines are not included unless the question explicitly asks for all fencing or all marked segments.

A rectangle has opposite sides equal, perimeter P = 2l + 2w, and area A = l*w. A square is a rectangle with l = w, so P = 4s and A = s^2. The units explain the area formula: multiplying a length by a perpendicular width counts a grid of unit squares. A parallelogram has A = b*h, where h is perpendicular to the chosen base, and its perimeter is 2a + 2b when a and b are adjacent side lengths. A slanted side is not automatically the height; the height is the shortest perpendicular distance between the parallel base lines.

A trapezoid, using a and b for its parallel bases and h for the perpendicular height, has A = (a + b)h/2. This is the average of the two parallel widths times the distance between them. The nonparallel legs are useful for perimeter but are not substituted for h unless a right-angle relationship makes one a height. Under the inclusive convention from the polygon lesson, a parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides and also qualifies as a trapezoid; use the formula that best matches the information and the stated figure.

The units must be aligned before arithmetic. Convert 100 cm to 1 m before finding an area in square metres. For area conversions, square the length conversion: 1 m^2 = 10,000 cm^2. A perimeter conversion uses the ordinary factor: 1 m = 100 cm. Write the unit after each intermediate result so a length does not accidentally become an area. Exact fractions and decimals are valid; do not round unless requested.

Missing dimensions are inverse problems. From A = l*w, w = A/l. From P = 2l + 2w, w = P/2 - l. For a parallelogram, h = A/b. For a trapezoid, h = 2A/(a+b). Substitute a recovered dimension back into the original formula. A dimension must be positive for a nondegenerate figure; a zero or negative result signals inconsistent givens.

Composite figures can be solved by decomposition or subtraction. Draw a segment that splits an L-shape into two rectangles, add their areas, and add only the exposed outer edges for perimeter. Alternatively, surround a notched figure with a larger rectangle and subtract the missing rectangle. For a rectangle with a triangular corner removed, subtract the triangle area (base*height/2) and replace the removed straight boundary with the two new sloping or perpendicular edges when finding perimeter. Internal construction lines are scaffolding, not automatically boundary.

A composite perimeter often has cancellation opportunities. If a rectangular corner is removed from a larger rectangle, the lost horizontal and vertical pieces are replaced by equal-length new edges, so the perimeter can sometimes be found by walking every outside segment or by using the original perimeter plus the new exposed edge minus the removed edge. Do not assume this for a diagonal cut; a sloping edge has its own length and may require Pythagoras.

A reliable workflow is: identify the requested quantity; sketch or label all needed dimensions; convert units; choose a formula; solve for a missing dimension if needed; calculate each component; combine by addition or subtraction; and attach the correct unit. A 2D area is measured in cm^2, m^2, or another squared unit. A perimeter is measured in cm or m. A price per square metre multiplies an area, while a price per metre multiplies a perimeter.

Rotating or reflecting a figure leaves its perimeter and area unchanged. A floor plan drawn sideways is still governed by the same lengths. A sketch is not necessarily to scale; rely on labels, parallel marks, right-angle marks, and stated relationships. For a parallelogram, a base of 8 cm and slanted side 5 cm does not determine area until the perpendicular height is given. For a trapezoid, two bases without a height do not determine area.

Self-check: Did I trace only the outside for perimeter? Did I use a perpendicular height? Are all lengths in the same unit? Did I subtract a cutout exactly once? Are my final units linear or squared? Does the answer have a reasonable size compared with the enclosing figure?

skills.name: Pythagoras and coordinate distance
skills.description: Use the Pythagorean theorem only for right triangles, find exact distances on coordinates, and use the converse.
skills.theory:
The Pythagorean theorem belongs to right triangles. If the legs meet at the marked 90-degree angle and c is the side opposite that angle, the hypotenuse, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and is never one of the two legs. A label saying “triangle” is not enough; a right-angle mark or an explicitly stated right angle is required before applying the theorem.

To find a hypotenuse, add the squares of the legs and take the positive square root: c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2). To find a missing leg, subtract the known leg square from the hypotenuse square: a = sqrt(c^2 - b^2). The positive root is used for a length. Keep exact radicals when a square root is not an integer. For legs 5 and 12, c = sqrt(25+144) = 13. For legs 3 and 4, c = 5. For legs 6 and 8, c = 10. For legs 1 and 1, c = sqrt(2), which should not be changed to a rounded decimal unless requested.

The converse tests whether a triangle is right when all three side lengths are known. Put the longest side c first. If a^2 + b^2 = c^2, the triangle is right. If a^2 + b^2 > c^2, the largest angle is acute; if a^2 + b^2 < c^2, the largest angle is obtuse. The converse is a statement about side lengths and the angle opposite the longest side. Do not compare an arbitrary pair of sides or forget to identify the largest length.

A coordinate distance problem becomes a right triangle by drawing horizontal and vertical helper segments between two points. For A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2), the horizontal leg has length |x2-x1| and the vertical leg has length |y2-y1|. The distance is d = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). Absolute values give nonnegative leg lengths, but squaring makes the sign irrelevant in the final formula. A negative run or rise simply records direction; distance itself is positive.

Coordinate grids are visual aids, not permission to count inaccurately. Read the ordered pairs, subtract corresponding coordinates, and square both differences. The formula is symmetric: reversing A and B changes the signs but not the distance. Horizontal points with equal y have distance |delta x|, and vertical points with equal x have distance |delta y|. A point and the origin use d = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), which is the same right-triangle idea.

Exact form communicates structure. sqrt(50) simplifies to 5sqrt(2) because 50 = 25*2. sqrt(72) = 6sqrt(2). Do not write sqrt(50) as 25sqrt(2), and do not replace an exact radical with 7.07 when the prompt asks for exact form. A calculator approximation is useful for checking magnitude, but it is not the exact answer.

In a word problem, first decide whether the requested segment is a right-triangle hypotenuse, a leg, or a coordinate distance. A ladder against a vertical wall forms a right triangle only if the wall and ground are perpendicular. A diagonal of a rectangle is a hypotenuse because adjacent sides meet at right angles. A diagonal of a general parallelogram is not automatically covered by Pythagoras; extra right-angle information is needed. Similarly, an arbitrary triangle with three side lengths needs the converse or another theorem, not an invented right angle.

Visual justification is part of the method. Mark the right angle, draw the two helper legs, and name the hypotenuse opposite the right angle. Then write the equation before substituting numbers. Check that a computed hypotenuse is longer than either leg and that a computed leg is shorter than the hypotenuse. For coordinates, check whether the result is at least as large as each absolute coordinate change.

A visual proof can use a square dissection. Make a large square of side a+b and place four congruent right triangles with legs a and b around a central square of side c. The four triangles have total area 4(ab/2), so comparing the large square with its pieces gives (a+b)^2 = 4(ab/2) + c^2 and therefore a^2 + b^2 = c^2. For coordinate distance, the horizontal and vertical helper segments are the same perpendicular legs in this dissection idea.

Self-check: Is there an actual right angle? Did I put the longest side on the c^2 side? Did I use positive lengths and simplify radicals exactly? For a converse, did I compare the two shorter squares with the longest square? For coordinates, did I subtract x-values from x-values and y-values from y-values?
