skills.name: Rigid transformations, symmetry, and congruence
skills.description: Describe translations, rotations, reflections, and congruence using preserved measurements and correspondence.
skills.theory:
A transformation maps every point of a figure to an image point. The original is often called the preimage and the result the image; corresponding points can be named A and A'. A transformation description should say what happens to points, where it happens, and which measurements are preserved. A rigid transformation, also called an isometry, preserves distances and angle measures. It can move or turn a figure, but it cannot stretch, shrink, shear, or change the shape.

A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction. In coordinates, a translation by vector (h,k) sends (x,y) to (x+h,y+k). Corresponding segments remain parallel and equal in length, and the orientation is unchanged. A translation has no fixed point unless its vector is zero. To describe a translation clearly, give the horizontal and vertical change or a directed vector, not just “move right.”

A rotation turns a figure about a center through a directed angle. The center stays fixed, and every point travels along a circular arc centered there. A positive counterclockwise quarter-turn about the origin sends (x,y) to (-y,x); a half-turn sends (x,y) to (-x,-y). Rotations preserve distances, angles, and orientation, although the page direction changes. “Clockwise” and “counterclockwise” matter; a 90-degree turn in opposite directions gives different images.

A reflection flips a figure across a line called the line of reflection. Each point and its image lie on a perpendicular to the axis and are the same distance from it. Points on the axis are fixed. Reflection preserves lengths and angles but reverses orientation: a clockwise order becomes counterclockwise. Reflection over the x-axis sends (x,y) to (x,-y), and reflection over the y-axis sends (x,y) to (-x,y). A mirror line is a geometric object, not merely a visual crease.

Symmetry is a transformation that maps a figure onto itself. A line of symmetry is a reflection axis; rotational symmetry of order n means the figure matches itself after turns such as 360/n degrees, with the identity full turn excluded from the count. A square has four reflection axes and rotational symmetry of order 4. A non-square rectangle has two reflection axes and rotational symmetry of order 2. A general parallelogram has a 180-degree rotational symmetry but usually no reflection symmetry. A scalene triangle has no nontrivial symmetry.

Two figures are congruent when a rigid transformation or a sequence of rigid transformations maps one exactly onto the other. Congruence preserves all corresponding side lengths and angle measures. Correspondence must be explicit: if triangle ABC maps to A'B'C', then AB corresponds to A'B', angle B corresponds to angle B', and so on. A correct vertex order in a congruence statement encodes those matches. A congruent figure may be translated, rotated, or reflected and may face the opposite direction.

Triangle congruence can be established by SSS (three corresponding sides), SAS (two sides and their included angle), or ASA (two angles and their included side). AAS is also sufficient, since the third angle follows from the triangle sum, but this lesson uses SSS, SAS, and ASA as the core tests. SSA is not generally sufficient: two different triangles can share two side lengths and a non-included angle. An arbitrary visual overlap is not a proof of congruence.

Coordinate transformations are easiest when applied to every vertex. For a translation, add the same vector to each coordinate. For a reflection, change the coordinate named by the axis. For a rotation, use the rule or trace perpendicular distances from the center. Then check one or two distances to confirm the map. If all pairwise distances are preserved, the image is congruent even if the orientation changed.

A dilation is deliberately excluded from rigid motions because it changes lengths unless the scale factor is 1. A shape enlarged by factor 2 is similar to the original but not congruent. Likewise, a shear can preserve some parallel lines while changing angles and lengths, so it is not rigid. The words “same shape,” “same size,” and “same orientation” should be separated: congruence requires same size, while orientation may change.

Self-check: Did I name the center and direction for a rotation, the vector for a translation, or the axis for a reflection? Are point correspondences in the right order? Did I use a valid congruence criterion with an included angle for SAS? Did I reject SSA and resizing? Do preserved lengths and angles support the claim?

skills.name: Similarity, scale drawings, and scaling laws
skills.description: Recognize similar figures, use correspondence and scale factors, and connect length and area scaling to trigonometry.
skills.theory:
Similar figures have the same shape: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding side lengths are proportional. Their orientation may differ, and one may be larger or smaller. Congruent figures are the special case with scale factor 1. Similarity does not require equal size. A scale factor k from a source to an image multiplies every length by k. If k > 1 the image is enlarged; if 0 < k < 1 it is reduced. Lengths remain positive, so use a positive factor for ordinary scale drawings.

Correspondence is the foundation. If triangle ABC is similar to triangle A'B'C', the order says A matches A', B matches B', and C matches C'. Therefore AB/A'B' = BC/B'C' = AC/A'C', with the ratio direction kept consistent. A common error is to match sides by their page position or apparent length instead of by their opposite angles and vertex order. Label the correspondence before writing a proportion.

The triangle similarity criteria are AA, SAS, and SSS. AA requires two pairs of equal corresponding angles; the third pair follows from the triangle angle sum. SAS requires two proportional corresponding sides and the included angle equal. SSS requires all three pairs of corresponding sides in one common ratio. Unlike congruence, the lengths need not be equal. Three angles alone establish similarity by AA but do not establish congruence because the size can vary.

A scale drawing uses a fixed ratio between drawing length and real length. If 1 cm represents 4 m, then a 7 cm drawing segment represents 28 m. Write the units on both sides and multiply by the real-units-per-drawing-unit ratio. To find a drawing length, divide the real length by the same ratio. Mixed units must be converted first: 1 m is 100 cm, and the scale statement determines which direction the conversion runs.

Area scales by the square of the length factor. If all lengths multiply by k, then a rectangle's area changes from lw to (kl)(kw) = k^2 lw. A scale factor 3 gives nine times the area; a reduction by 1/2 gives one quarter the area. Surface materials therefore require a squared factor. Perimeter scales linearly by k because it adds lengths. Volume, when introduced later, scales by k^3; do not use that rule for a plane area.

For similar triangles, corresponding altitudes, medians, and other lengths also share factor k. If a small triangle has base 5 and its image has corresponding base 8, the factor is 8/5. A small area of 20 then becomes 20*(8/5)^2 = 20*64/25 = 256/5 square units. Keep an exact fraction when the scale factor is not an integer. A perimeter of 18 becomes 18*(8/5) = 144/5.

Parallel lines create useful similar triangles. When a segment is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, corresponding angles are equal, giving AA similarity. This is the bridge from angle relationships to proportional lengths. The same idea supports shadows: a vertical object and its shadow form a triangle similar to a shorter reference object and its shadow when the sun rays are treated as parallel. The ratio compares corresponding heights and shadow lengths, not arbitrary pairs.

Trigonometry later packages the same right-triangle correspondences into sine, cosine, and tangent. Similar right triangles with the same acute angle have a constant ratio of opposite to hypotenuse, for example, so a scale change preserves the trigonometric ratio. A triangle can be similar without being right, but a trig ratio must be matched to the chosen angle and sides. Similarity is the geometric reason a ratio stays stable across different-sized right triangles.

Similarity is not a license to assume proportionality from appearance. A diagram may be compressed on a screen. Use stated equal angles, parallel marks, side ratios, or a scale statement. A dilation changes size while preserving shape and angles; a rigid transformation preserves size as well. If two figures share only one angle and one side, there is not enough information for a general similarity conclusion.

Self-check: Did I write the correspondence in the correct order? Are my proportions oriented consistently? Did I distinguish similarity from congruence? Did I square the length factor for area but use the first power for perimeter? Did I convert scale units and connect any trig ratio to the same angle?

skills.name: Circle areas, sectors, annuli, and composite circular regions
skills.description: Find exact and approximate areas of disks, sectors, annuli, and composite circular regions while keeping radius, diameter, and arc length distinct.
skills.theory:
A circle is a boundary; the disk is the filled region inside it. In area questions, the object is usually the
disk, so the formula is A = pi r^2. The radius r runs from the centre to the boundary. A diameter d runs all
the way across the centre, so d = 2r and r = d/2. Substituting a diameter directly into pi r^2 produces an
answer four times too large. Before calculating, label every given length as radius, diameter, circumference,
or arc length. Those measurements describe different geometric features.

Exact form preserves pi. If r = 6, the disk area is 36pi square units, not 113.04 square units. The exact form
displays the structure and can be compared without rounding. A decimal is useful when a context asks for an
estimate; then choose a stated value such as pi approximately 3.14159 and label the result with square units.
Do not mix an exact coefficient with an unannounced decimal. A useful size check is that a disk of radius 6 has
area a little more than 36 times 3, so a result near 113 is plausible.

Circle arc and angle work from MATH_GEOM_002 is optional bridge context: this lesson uses the same central-angle fraction while focusing on filled area.

  A sector is a slice bounded by two radii and an arc. If its central angle is theta degrees, it is theta/360 of
a full turn, so its area is A_sector = (theta/360)pi r^2. A 90-degree sector is one quarter of the disk, and a
180-degree sector is a semicircle. The angle must be central: an angle measured at another point may not select
the same fraction. When theta is in radians, the fraction is theta/(2pi), giving A_sector = (1/2)r^2 theta.
Keep degree and radian formulas separate; inserting 90 into the radian formula is a unit error.

An annulus is the ring between two concentric circles. Let R be the outer radius and r the inner radius. Its
area is the large disk minus the hole: A_annulus = pi R^2 - pi r^2 = pi(R^2-r^2). Subtract squared radii,
not radii. If the problem gives outer and inner diameters, halve both before squaring. The inner circle is a
hole, so its area is excluded even though its boundary may still be part of a perimeter question.

Composite circular regions combine pieces. Add non-overlapping sectors and disks, or subtract holes and cutouts.
A washer with a rectangular tab has area pi(R^2-r^2) + LW only when the tab and ring do not overlap. A repeated
pattern of equal sectors can often be recognized as a full disk: four quarter-disks have total area pi r^2.
State which boundaries are shared; a shared boundary changes perimeter bookkeeping, but it does not create extra
area. A diagram is a plan for the decomposition, not a scale drawing to measure with a ruler.

Area scales quadratically. If every length is multiplied by k, every disk, sector, and annulus area is multiplied
by k^2. Doubling a radius quadruples area; tripling it multiplies area by nine. This is why two circles can have
equal central angles but different arc lengths and areas: the radius controls the scale. Arc length scales by k,
while area scales by k^2. Confusing these scaling laws is a common source of answers that have the wrong size.

A reliable workflow is: draw or read the centre and boundaries; convert diameter to radius; choose disk, sector,
annulus, or a sum/difference of pieces; substitute into an exact formula; simplify the coefficient of pi; then
approximate only if requested. Check that the answer is nonnegative, that a sector is no larger than the whole
disk when its angle is at most 360 degrees, and that an annulus is smaller than its outer disk. Report square
units. A boundary curve can have a length while the filled region has an area; use the requested dimension and
  units rather than borrowing the circumference formula. For a composite drawing, mark each piece once and cancel
  overlaps only when they truly share interior. The reviewed capstone asks for an exact coefficient of pi, an
  approximation, and a decomposition explanation.

examples.prompt: Find the exact area of a disk with radius 7.
examples.explanation: Use A = pi r^2, so A = pi(7^2) = 49pi.

examples.prompt: A circle has diameter 18. Find its exact area.
examples.explanation: The radius is 9, so A = pi(9^2) = 81pi. Using 18 as the radius would be four times too large.

examples.prompt: Find the area of a 90-degree sector with radius 10.
examples.explanation: A quarter of pi(10^2) is 100pi/4 = 25pi.

examples.explanation: The fraction is 120/360 = 1/3, so (1/3)pi(36) = 12pi.

examples.prompt: Find the exact area of an annulus with outer radius 9 and inner radius 5.
examples.explanation: Subtract disks: pi(9^2-5^2) = pi(81-25) = 56pi.

examples.prompt: A ring has outer diameter 20 and inner diameter 12. Find its area.
examples.explanation: The radii are 10 and 6, so pi(100-36) = 64pi.

examples.prompt: Four non-overlapping 90-degree sectors have radius 4. What is their combined area?
examples.explanation: Four quarters make one disk, so the total is pi(4^2) = 16pi.

examples.prompt: A disk of radius 3 is enlarged so every length is multiplied by 5. How does its area change?
examples.explanation: Area scales by the square of the length scale: 5^2 = 25.

examples.prompt: A 60-degree sector has radius 12. Give its area as a multiple of pi.
A circular sign has radius 8 and a concentric circular cutout of radius 3. Estimate the remaining area using pi approximately 3.14159.
examples.explanation: The exact area is pi(64-9) = 55pi; multiplying by 3.14159 gives 172.78745.

skills.name: Volume and surface area of prisms and cylinders
skills.description: Calculate volume and surface area for cubes, cuboids, right prisms, and cylinders using nets, exposed faces, capacity, and scaling.
skills.theory:
Volume measures how much three-dimensional space an object occupies. It is counted in cubic units because three
independent lengths are multiplied. A cuboid with length L, width W, and height H has V = LWH. A cube with
side s has V = s^3. Capacity is the same physical volume reported in a container unit: 1 litre = 1,000 cubic
centimetres and 1 millilitre = 1 cubic centimetre. Keep the unit conversion attached to the answer; a numerical
result without units can hide a factor of 1,000 error.

A right prism has two congruent, parallel bases and a constant cross-section between them. If the base area is
B and the prism length or height is H, V = BH. A rectangular prism uses B = LW. A triangular or polygonal base
can be handled by finding its base area first, but this lesson focuses on cubes, cuboids, and right prisms with a
supplied base area. The word right means the connecting edges are perpendicular to the bases, so the stated
height is the perpendicular distance, not a slanted edge.

Surface area measures the total area of exposed faces. A cuboid has two faces of each dimension, so SA = 2LW +
2LH + 2WH. A cube has six equal square faces, SA = 6s^2. A net unfolds every face into a flat arrangement. Adding
the areas of all net faces once is a reliable method. Shared edges appear in the net as joins, but they are not
extra surface area. If a box is open at the top, omit only the top face; if it is placed on a floor, decide whether
the question asks total surface area or only the exposed area.

For a right prism whose base perimeter is P, the lateral area is PH. Add the two bases to obtain total surface
area: SA = PH + 2B. This decomposition prevents a frequent mistake: using volume BH when the problem asks for
the outside covering. A rectangular prism illustrates both formulas. Its lateral area is 2(L+W)H and its bases
contribute 2LW, giving the cuboid formula after expansion.

A cylinder is a right prism with circular bases. Its volume is V = pi r^2 h. Its total surface area is the two
circular bases plus the curved side: SA = 2pi r^2 + 2pi rh. The curved side unwraps to a rectangle of width 2pi r
and height h. A cylinder net therefore has two circles and one rectangle. Use radius, not diameter, in r^2; halve
a stated diameter first. For exact work leave pi; for a decimal, state the approximation. A can with a lid and a
base has both circles exposed only when the context calls for the complete outside surface.

Exposed faces depend on the physical situation. A cube joined to another cube has a shared face hidden inside, so
the two cubes contribute 12 faces minus 2 hidden faces = 10 exposed square faces. A stack of n cubes in a straight
column has 6n - 2(n-1) exposed faces because each join hides two faces. A cuboid against a wall may have one face
excluded from painting. State the model before calculating; “surface area” alone usually means every outside face.

Scaling is cubic for volume and quadratic for surface area. Multiplying every length by k multiplies volume by
k^3 and surface area by k^2. Doubling a box makes eight times as much room but only four times as much covering.
This distinction matters in packaging, storage, and material estimates. A quick check compares dimensions: a box
with sides 2, 3, and 4 has volume 24, while its surface area is 52; the two quantities cannot share units.

A careful workflow is: identify the solid and the requested quantity; label base, height, radius, and diameter;
choose a formula; preserve exact pi when useful; convert units at the end; and check whether a face is hidden or
omitted. Draw a net for surface area and a cross-section for volume. The reviewed capstone asks for volume,
surface area, capacity, and a sentence explaining why the units and faces differ.

skills.name: Shifted and scaled absolute-value equations and inequalities
skills.description: Solve and interpret shifted and scaled absolute-value equations and inequalities, including two, one, and no solutions with exact interval endpoints.
skills.theory:
Absolute value measures distance, so |x-h| is the distance from x to the centre h on a number line. The graph
of y = |x| is a V with vertex (0,0). Replacing x by x-h moves the vertex to h, and adding k moves it vertically
to (h,k). A positive scale a in y = a|x-h|+k changes the steepness; it does not move the vertex. A negative
a reflects the V downward. These shifts are easiest to read from the inside and outside separately: h is the
horizontal centre, k is the vertical baseline, and a is a stretch or reflection.

To solve a shifted equation, isolate the absolute value before splitting cases. For a|x-h|+k = m with a nonzero,
first calculate d = (m-k)/a. The equation becomes |x-h| = d. If d > 0, there are two solutions h-d and h+d.
If d = 0, there is one solution x=h. If d < 0, there are no real solutions because a distance cannot be
negative. If a is negative, dividing by a reverses the comparison in an inequality and may change whether the
resulting condition is “inside” or “outside.” Always inspect the sign rather than memorizing one pattern.

The equation |x-h| = d says “x is exactly d units from h.” It therefore gives two endpoints when d is positive.
An equation with a tolerance, |x-h| <= d, means the distance is at most d and gives the closed interval
[h-d,h+d]. A strict inequality |x-h| < d gives the open interval (h-d,h+d). For a lower bound, |x-h| >= d,
the solution is outside the central interval: (-inf,h-d] union [h+d,inf) when equality is included. With >,
both endpoints are open. Endpoint brackets are part of the answer: equality includes the point, while a strict
sign excludes it.

Scaled inequalities follow the same isolation step. If a is positive, a|x-h| <= m-k becomes |x-h| <=
(m-k)/a. If a is negative, dividing reverses the sign; the shape can turn a bounded “within” condition into an
unbounded outside condition. Before taking roots or drawing an interval, check whether the resulting threshold is
positive, zero, or negative. For example, -2|x-3|+5 >= 1 gives |x-3| <= 2, so x belongs to [1,5]. In contrast,
-2|x-3|+5 <= 1 gives |x-3| >= 2, so x is outside [1,5].

A negative threshold exposes the range of the model. Since |x-h| >= 0, the expression a|x-h|+k has minimum k
when a>0 and maximum k when a<0. An equation asking a positive-scale V to equal below k has no solutions;
asking it to equal k has one vertex solution. An inequality can become all real numbers or the empty set. “No
solution” and “all real numbers” are different conclusions and should be written explicitly, not approximated by
an interval with a guessed endpoint.

Tolerances model measurement and control. If a sensor target is h and the allowed error is d, then
|x-h| <= d is a within band. If a safety rule rejects values too close to a target, |x-h| > d is an outside
band. A shifted and scaled graph lets you read the same decision geometrically: horizontal intersections locate
equation solutions, and horizontal strips translate into intervals on the x-axis. Use exact fractions when the
data are exact; use a declared decimal tolerance only when the prompt requests an approximation.

A reliable workflow is: identify a, h, k, and the comparison value; isolate the absolute value; classify the
threshold; choose two points, one point, no points, a central interval, an outside union, all reals, or empty set;
then verify an endpoint in the original expression. The reviewed capstone requires the interval, endpoint checks,
and a verbal explanation of why the inequality is within or outside the tolerance band. In a graph, the horizontal coordinate is the constrained input and the vertical value is the model output. Check one interior point and one exterior point when reading intervals; those substitutions expose a reversed inequality or misplaced shift before submission.

skills.name: Higher roots and rational exponents
skills.description: Interpret higher-index roots and rational exponents over the reals, including principal roots, equation solutions, negative powers, domains, exact forms, and approximations.
skills.theory:
The nth root of a is a number whose nth power is a. The index n is written on the radical: n√a. When n is even,
the real radical is defined only for a >= 0, and the principal root is the nonnegative value. Thus √49 = 7 and
the principal fourth root of 81 is 3. The radical symbol names one principal value; it does not automatically
mean plus or minus. When n is odd, every real radicand has one real nth root, including negative values: the real
cube root of -8 is -2 because (-2)^3 = -8.

Root notation and equation solving ask different questions. The statement √49 = 7 names the principal root. The
equation x^2 = 49 asks for every real x whose square is 49, so x = -7 or x = 7. Likewise, the principal fourth
root of 16 is 2, but x^4 = 16 has x = -2 and x = 2 in the real numbers. For an odd power, x^3 = -8 has only
x = -2 because an odd-power function is one-to-one on the reals. Add a plus-or-minus only when the equation and
the even power justify it.

Rational exponents encode roots and powers. For a positive base a, a^(m/n) means (n√a)^m, equivalently the
nth root of a^m. The denominator n is the root index and the numerator m is the power. For example,
16^(3/4) = (fourth root of 16)^3 = 2^3 = 8, while 27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)^2 = 9. Reduce the fraction
when possible, but preserve the domain. Exact perfect powers are preferable in exact questions; leave an answer
such as 2^(1/3) in radical or exponent form when no simpler real form exists.

Negative rational exponents mean reciprocals: a^(-m/n) = 1/a^(m/n), provided the base is nonzero. For instance,
8^(-2/3) = 1/(cube root of 8)^2 = 1/4. The base cannot be zero because a negative power divides by the positive
power. A negative base requires care. Odd denominators can describe a real odd root, while even denominators
require a nonnegative radicand under the real-number convention. Do not let a calculator’s complex or language-
specific fractional-power behavior silently change the real domain.

Domain restrictions follow the root index and any denominator. An expression such as fourth root of (x-3) is
real only when x-3 >= 0, so its domain is [3,inf). An odd root of (2x+1) accepts every real x. An expression
(x-4)^(-1/3) accepts every real x except 4, because the odd root exists at every input but the reciprocal would
divide by zero. For an even root in a denominator, combine both conditions: the radicand must be positive, not
merely nonnegative, because zero would make the denominator zero.

For a negative base, state the convention before using a rational exponent: reduce the fraction to lowest terms, and treat an odd denominator as an odd root in the real numbers. Do not assume that a nested even-root rewrite is interchangeable with a real odd root. For example, ((-8)^2)^(1/6) = 2, while the real cube root expression (-8)^(1/3) = -2. The positive-base laws agree more freely because all intermediate roots stay in the positive domain; negative bases need the parity and domain check first.

  Simplification must respect signs. For even roots, √(x^2) = |x|, not x for every real x, because the principal
root is nonnegative. For odd roots, cube root of (x^3) = x for every real x. This parity distinction explains
why an algebraic cancellation that looks identical can have different real meanings. Check by raising the proposed
principal value back to the index and by checking its sign.

Approximation is appropriate when the exact root is not a convenient rational or radical. Bracket a root between
nearby perfect powers: 2^3=8 and 3^3=27, so cube root of 20 lies between 2 and 3. A decimal answer should state
the requested precision and a tolerance. Keep exact and approximate forms visibly distinct. A negative odd root
can be approximated by first finding the positive magnitude and then restoring the negative sign, rather than
relying on a floating-language expression whose branch convention may be complex.

A reliable workflow is: identify the index and parity; decide whether the task asks for a principal radical or all
equation solutions; translate rational exponents into roots and powers; apply reciprocal and domain restrictions;
simplify exactly; and approximate only at the end. The reviewed capstone asks for both the principal-root statement
and the complete equation solution, with a domain and sign explanation.

skills.name: Derivatives as local rates and limits
skills.description: Connect secant slopes, difference quotients, finite two-sided limits, tangent lines, and instantaneous rates; distinguish point values, approximation, and failure of differentiability.
skills.theory:
A derivative describes local change. An average rate uses two distinct inputs; a derivative asks what those rates approach as the second input moves toward the first. This lesson connects the difference quotients and limits you already know. All functions and derivatives here are real. An ordinary derivative means a finite, two-sided derivative at an interior point unless a question explicitly asks about one-sided behavior.


From a secant to a local rate:
For a function f and distinct inputs a and a+h, the average rate is [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h. The numerator is a change in output, not the output itself. The denominator is a change in input and may be positive or negative, but it is not zero. On a graph this quotient is the slope of a secant through two points. As h approaches zero, the points approach each other. If the quotients approach one common finite value, that value is f'(a).


The definition:
f'(a) = lim as h -> 0 of [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h.
A prime does not mean multiplication, an inverse function, or a reciprocal. If y=f(x), dy/dx is another notation for the derivative. At this stage treat it as derivative notation, not permission to cancel arbitrary symbols. A derivative at a point is a number. The derivative function f'(x) assigns that number at each input where it exists.


A complete first-principles calculation:
Let f(x)=x^2 and a=3. Then f(3+h)=(3+h)^2 and f(3)=9. The quotient is [(3+h)^2-9]/h. Expanding the numerator gives 6h+h^2. For h!=0, division gives 6+h. Only now take the limit: f'(3)=6. The excluded increment remains excluded from the original quotient. A limit of 6 does not turn division by zero into a valid operation.


The same calculation at a general input gives [(a+h)^2-a^2]/h=2a+h for h!=0, so the derivative function of x^2 is 2x. At a=-2 it is -4; at zero it is zero. The graph can have a horizontal tangent at one point without being a constant function. A tangent need not touch the graph only once or stay entirely on one side of it: y=0 is tangent to y=x^3 at zero and the curve crosses it there.


Other definitions-based examples:
For f(x)=mx+b, the output change is mh, so every nonzero-increment quotient equals m. A constant output has zero output change and derivative zero. For x^3, expansion gives [ (a+h)^3-a^3 ]/h=3a^2+3ah+h^2 for h!=0, hence the derivative at a is 3a^2. These results are consequences of the definition, not rules that should be invoked when an exercise specifically asks for first principles.


Roots and reciprocals:
For sqrt(x) at a=4, multiply the difference quotient by the conjugate. On nearby allowed inputs, [sqrt(4+h)-2]/h becomes 1/[sqrt(4+h)+2], whose limit is 1/4. At a general positive a the corresponding result is 1/[2sqrt(a)]. For 1/x at a!=0, combine the numerator fractions to obtain -1/[a(a+h)] for h!=0 and a+h!=0. The limit is -1/a^2. State the function's original domain as well as the increment restriction.


When the derivative fails:
For f(x)=abs(x) at zero, the difference quotient is abs(h)/h. It equals -1 to the left and 1 to the right. The two-sided derivative does not exist because the sides disagree. Continuity alone therefore does not guarantee differentiability. Conversely, differentiability at an interior point implies continuity there. A jump, an unfilled hole, or a reassigned point value can prevent differentiability even when a nearby simplified curve looks smooth.


At an endpoint such as zero for sqrt(x), this lesson does not invent a missing real left neighborhood. Even the right-hand quotient equals 1/sqrt(h) for h>0 and grows without bound. That is not a finite ordinary derivative. Keep a finite slope, unequal one-sided slopes, an undefined function value, and unbounded one-sided slope conceptually separate.


Interpretation and approximation:
If s measures position in metres and t measures time in seconds, s'(a) has units metres per second. Its sign indicates direction in that coordinate, not whether the position itself is positive. A negative temperature derivative means cooling; it does not imply a negative temperature. For small delta, f(a+delta) is approximately f(a)+f'(a)*delta when the local linear model is appropriate. This is an approximation, not a claim that every curved graph is a line.


The tangent through (a,f(a)) has equation y=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a). The point value locates the line and the derivative controls its slope. Do not substitute f(a) for the slope. Numerical tables and graphs help form and check conjectures, but finitely many samples alone do not establish a limit. In the formal exercise, prove the exact punctured limit first, then cite it with derivative_from_limit. A shortcut polynomial derivative is not evidence that you used the requested definition.

Before calculating, identify the original function, evaluation point, and increment separately.

skills.name: Power, constant, and sum rules
skills.description: Differentiate real polynomials using justified elementary rules, evaluate rates and tangents, and distinguish stationary inputs from roots and extrema.
skills.theory:
The derivative definition explains what a derivative means. Differentiation rules let us calculate efficiently once that meaning is established. This lesson develops constant, constant-multiple, sum, difference, and nonnegative integer-power rules. Its functions are polynomials, so their domains and derivative domains are all real numbers. Products of nonconstant functions, quotients with variable denominators, and unexpanded nested functions belong to later lessons.


Constants and identity:
A constant function f(x)=c has derivative zero because f(a+h)-f(a)=c-c=0 for every permitted increment. The identity function f(x)=x has derivative one because its output change equals its input change. Consequently an affine function mx+b has derivative m. Here m and b are constant with respect to x. Saying that a letter is constant must be part of the problem, not a guess based on its appearance.


The power rule:
For a positive integer n, the derivative of x^n is n*x^(n-1). The exponent becomes a coefficient and then decreases by one. For x^5 this produces 5x^4, not x^4, 5x^5, or x^6. For n=1 the result is one. Handle an explicitly constant function separately rather than mechanically writing 0*x^(-1) and creating an artificial exception at zero. The constant-one function has derivative zero at every real input.


Why the rule is reasonable:
The definition for x^n starts with [(a+h)^n-a^n]/h. In the binomial expansion, the a^n terms cancel. The next term is n*a^(n-1)*h; every remaining term contains at least h^2. Dividing for h!=0 leaves n*a^(n-1) plus terms containing h, which approach zero. This explains both the coefficient n and the reduced exponent. The rules are connected to limits, not a new meaning of equality.


Constant multiples and addition:
The derivative of c*f(x) is c*f'(x) when c is constant. The derivative of f(x)+g(x) is f'(x)+g'(x), and subtraction works similarly, provided the component derivatives exist at the point. These statements follow by distributing the difference quotient and applying finite-limit laws. Preserve coefficients and signs before simplifying. For 4x^3-5x+8, the derivative is 12x^2-5. The constant 8 disappears, but the coefficient 4 does not.


An organized calculation:
Identify the variable first. Split a polynomial into terms with their signs. Differentiate each term using a stated rule. Combine the derivative terms, then evaluate at a point if requested. For p(t)=2t^4-3t^2+7, p'(t)=8t^3-6t. At t=-1, this is -8+6=-2. Substituting into p itself gives a position or output, not a rate. Substituting too early can erase the variable and lead to differentiating an already evaluated constant.


Representation matters:
Some expressions become polynomials after a justified expansion. To differentiate (x+3)^2 without a chain rule, first expand it to x^2+6x+9, then differentiate to 2x+6. Likewise x^2/4 is (1/4)*x^2, so its derivative is x/2. Division by a nonzero numerical constant is only constant multiplication. This does not license differentiating x^2/(x+4) by ignoring the variable denominator.


Derivative values and tangent lines:
Once a derivative function is known, evaluate it at the required input. For f(x)=x^3 at x=2, f(2)=8 and f'(2)=12, so the tangent is y=8+12(x-2). Its intercept is not obtained by confusing the input, output, and slope. A tangent formula should pass through the original point and use the derivative slope. Equivalent expanded and point-slope expressions describe the same line.


Graphs and stationary points:
Where a smooth graph slopes upward its derivative is positive, and where it slopes downward its derivative is negative. A stationary point has derivative zero. Solve f'(x)=0 to find candidates, not f(x)=0. For x^2-4x+1 the stationary input is 2, while the function's roots are different. A zero derivative at one point does not prove that the function is constant or that a maximum or minimum occurs there. The function x^3 has derivative zero at zero but keeps increasing through it. Classifying extrema rigorously is a later lesson.


Parameter and data problems:
Differentiation can determine an unknown constant. If f(x)=k*x^3 and f'(2)=36, then 12k=36 and k=3. When only derivative data are given, use the linearity rules directly: if f'(a)=u and g'(a)=v, then the derivative of 2f-3g at a is 2u-3v. No formula for f or g is needed. However, function values cannot substitute for derivative values.


Units and communication:
If a model gives distance in metres at time t seconds, its derivative is in metres per second. A constant offset changes the position graph but not the velocity. Multiplying every output by a constant multiplies its derivative by that same constant. Explain the operation being used rather than writing f=f', which is generally false. Algebraic equalities connect equivalent derivative expressions only after the differentiation step has been justified.


Scope and self-check:
Ask whether every exponent is an allowed integer, whether coefficients are constant, whether signs survived, and whether the question wants a function, a value, or a tangent. General rational powers and transcendental functions require additional hypotheses or rules. The formal polynomial exercise checks the stated derivative mathematically; the separately reviewed capstone checks your explanation and interpretation. Neither an answer-key phrase nor unexplained working establishes those objectives.

skills.name: Product and quotient rules
skills.description: Differentiate products and quotients with explicit hypotheses, retain original domains after cancellation, and interpret product and quotient rates in context.
skills.theory:
Products and quotients describe interacting quantities. Area can be length times width, and an average cost is total cost divided by output. When both components change, a derivative must account for both changes. The sum rule does not extend by simply multiplying or dividing derivatives. This lesson uses polynomials and rational functions, with the original real domain kept visible throughout.

The product rule:
If u and v are differentiable at an interior point, then (uv)'=u'v+uv'. One term describes change in u while retaining the current value of v; the other describes change in v while retaining the current value of u. Both original functions still appear. For (x+2)(x+5), the derivative is 1*(x+5)+(x+2)*1=2x+7. Multiplying the two derivatives would give 1, which misses almost all the change.

Why there are two terms:
Consider a rectangle of dimensions u and v whose side changes are du and dv. Its area change is v*du+u*dv+du*dv. Dividing by the input change gives two main contributions and a small cross term. For differentiable side functions, the cross term tends to zero in the limiting calculation. Equivalently, add and subtract u(a+h)*v(a) in the difference quotient and use continuity of differentiable functions. This explanation needs differentiability; it is not a rule for arbitrary discontinuous quantities.

An organized product calculation:
For f(x)=x^2(3x-4), choose u=x^2 and v=3x-4. Then u'=2x and v'=3. Apply the product rule before simplifying: f'=2x(3x-4)+3x^2=9x^2-8x. Expanding f to 3x^3-4x^2 first gives the same derivative by the power and sum rules. Either route is legitimate when the problem does not prescribe a method. The explicit two-term setup is useful evidence that you understand the product rule.

The quotient rule:
If u and v are differentiable at a and v(a)!=0, then the derivative of u/v at a is [u'(a)*v(a)-u(a)*v'(a)]/[v(a)]^2. For a derivative function, use the same formula wherever the hypotheses hold. The order of subtraction matters. The denominator is the original denominator squared, not the derivative of that denominator. Write the numerator in parentheses before reducing it.

A quotient example:
For f(x)=(x^2+1)/(x+1), the original domain excludes -1. Set u=x^2+1 and v=x+1. The derivative is [2x(x+1)-(x^2+1)]/(x+1)^2=(x^2+2x-1)/(x+1)^2, still for x!=-1. At x=1 the derivative equals (1+2-1)/4=1/2. The function value there is 1. Those two numbers have different roles in a tangent equation: y=1+(1/2)(x-1).

A way to remember the quotient structure:
The identity u=(u/v)*v holds where v is nonzero. Applying the product rule there gives u'=(u/v)'*v+(u/v)*v'. Rearranging yields the quotient formula. This is a useful consistency check once differentiability of the reciprocal has been established; it should not be presented as a circular existence proof. The reciprocal limit calculation from the first derivative lesson provides the missing foundation.

Simple special cases:
For c/(x+b), where c and b are constants, the derivative is -c/(x+b)^2 on x!=-b. For x/(x+b), it is b/(x+b)^2. A fixed numerical denominator such as x^3/5 is better viewed as (1/5)*x^3 and differentiated by constant multiplication. Select the simplest valid representation rather than mechanically use the longest available rule.

Original domains survive simplification:
The function (x^2-4)/(x-2) agrees with x+2 only where x!=2. It therefore has derivative 1 at every allowed input, but has no derivative at 2 because its value is undefined there. The extended function x+2 does have derivative 1 at 2; that is a different function. A cancelled factor in a derivative formula cannot restore a missing point in the original domain. Record restrictions before reducing either the function or its derivative.

Data without formulas:
Suppose u(a)=2, u'(a)=3, v(a)=5, and v'(a)=7. Then (uv)'(a)=3*5+2*7=29, while (u/v)'(a)=(3*5-2*7)/25=1/25. All four values are needed in general. The expression u'(a)/v'(a)=3/7 is neither the quotient derivative nor a substitute for it. When v(a)=0 the quotient is not defined at a, regardless of whether a simplified expression has a limit.

Applications and units:
If L(t) and W(t) are lengths in metres with t in seconds, A'(t)=L'(t)W(t)+L(t)W'(t) has units square metres per second. One side can grow while the other shrinks, so the signs of both contributions matter. If C(q) is total cost and q is output quantity, the average cost C(q)/q has derivative [q*C'(q)-C(q)]/q^2 for q>0 in the model. This is not the same quantity as the marginal total cost C'(q).

Limits of the rules:
A nonzero denominator alone is not sufficient; differentiability of the components must also be established. For example, abs(x-1)/(x+1) is defined at 1 but has unequal one-sided slopes there. Conversely, a particular product can be differentiable even if the usual rule's component hypotheses fail, so do not infer a converse. The lesson focuses on applying sufficient hypotheses correctly.

Self-check and proof:
Before calculating, identify u, v, their derivatives, and the original domain. After calculating, check signs, parentheses, units, and a simple sample value. A graph may reveal a sign error but is not a proof. The formal exercise checks one exact quotient derivative with its nonzero denominator; the reviewed capstone separately asks you to distinguish an original rational function from a continuous extension. Neither task replaces the other.

skills.name: The chain rule and composite functions
skills.description: Differentiate nested power, reciprocal, and square-root functions; combine rules, match outer derivative inputs, and preserve function and derivative domains.
skills.theory:
A composite function applies one operation to the result of another. Its derivative is therefore a rate through two linked stages. This lesson connects the function-composition work you already know to differentiation. We start with powers of affine and polynomial expressions, then include reciprocals and explicitly explained square roots. Exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric derivative rules are not assumed here.

Inner and outer functions:
For y=(3x+2)^4, choose u=g(x)=3x+2 and f(u)=u^4. The outer derivative is f'(u)=4u^3 and the inner derivative is g'(x)=3. The chain rule gives (f composed with g)'(x)=f'(g(x))*g'(x)=12(3x+2)^3. Evaluate the outer derivative at the inner output, not at x by default. Forgetting the factor 3 changes the rate.

Hypotheses:
At an input a, g must be differentiable at a and f must be differentiable at g(a). The composition must also be meaningful on the relevant nearby inputs. The formula is a sufficient-condition rule; failure of one hypothesis means this route does not apply automatically, not that no specially simplified composite can ever be differentiable. Check the point at which each component is evaluated.

Why rates multiply:
A small input change delta x produces approximately g'(a)*delta x change in the inner output. Near g(a), the outer function converts a small inner-output change into approximately f'(g(a)) times that change. Combining the local linear approximations gives f'(g(a))*g'(a)*delta x. This is the intuitive reason for multiplication. It is not an instruction to cancel derivative symbols without hypotheses, and a full proof must handle zero inner changes as well.

Power composites:
For [g(x)]^n with positive integer n, the derivative is n*[g(x)]^(n-1)*g'(x). For (x^2+4)^3 it is 3(x^2+4)^2*(2x)=6x(x^2+4)^2. Do not replace the exponent by n-1 and forget either multiplier. Factored answers are often clearer than a long expansion. A small polynomial example can be checked by expansion as an independent calculation, but expansion becomes inefficient for a high outer power.

More than two layers:
For [(2x+1)^2+3]^2, work from outside inward. The derivative is 2[(2x+1)^2+3] times 2(2x+1) times 2. Each stage has its own input. Keep the original inner expressions in place while differentiating one layer at a time. A dependency sketch with named intermediate quantities can prevent evaluating a derivative at the wrong point.

The square-root outer rule:
For positive u, the derivative of sqrt(u) is 1/[2sqrt(u)], as the conjugate difference-quotient calculation shows. Thus sqrt(g(x)) has derivative g'(x)/[2sqrt(g(x))] wherever g is differentiable and g(x)>0. For sqrt(3x+1), the function is defined for x>=-1/3, but this rule gives a finite ordinary derivative only for x>-1/3. At x=1 the derivative is 3/4. A function domain and a derivative domain need not be identical.

Special boundary behavior:
The requirement g(x)>0 belongs to this sufficient formula. At a zero of g, analyze the particular function rather than declare every possibility identical. For example, sqrt(x^2)=abs(x), which has a corner at zero. In contrast, sqrt(x^4)=x^2 is differentiable there. Do not divide by sqrt(0) in either case. This distinction prevents a formal-looking formula from being used outside its hypotheses.

Reciprocal composites:
The derivative of 1/g(x) is -g'(x)/[g(x)]^2 where g(x)!=0 and g is differentiable. It follows either from the quotient rule with numerator 1 or from the chain rule using the reciprocal outer function. For 1/(2x+5), the derivative is -2/(2x+5)^2 for x!=-5/2. The original pole remains excluded even when later algebra cancels a factor in a larger expression.

Combining rules:
For x*(x^2+1)^3, the top-level operation is multiplication, so start with the product rule. The derivative is (x^2+1)^3+x*3(x^2+1)^2*(2x). Chain-rule work occurs inside the second product term. For a quotient whose denominator is a composite power, use the quotient rule at the top level and the chain rule to differentiate that denominator. Naming the top-level operation is often the most useful first step.

Tables and contexts:
Suppose g(2)=5, g'(2)=3, f'(5)=7, and f'(2)=11. The derivative of f(g(x)) at 2 is 7*3=21, not 11*3. The value 5 tells us where to look up the outer derivative. If depth changes in metres per second and temperature changes in degrees per metre at that depth, multiplying the rates gives degrees per second. Units make the input-output link visible, but the rates must refer to the same location and instant.

Graphs, interpretation, and self-check:
A graph of the composite can help check the sign and approximate scale of a derivative. It cannot justify an unstated domain extension. Keep the derivative function distinct from its value at a point, and the function's value distinct from both. Explain the inner and outer functions, check where the rule applies, form the derivative, then substitute. The formal reference uses a nested square-root composite with an exact positive radicand. Its certificate verifies the mathematical conclusion, while the separate reviewed task assesses your explicit chain-rule explanation and domain reasoning. There is no claim that a generic certificate enforces an unrestricted teaching-method rubric.

skills.name: Angles, bearings, and degree measure
skills.description: Measure rotation in degrees, distinguish direction from orientation, and use bearings as angular descriptions of location.
skills.theory:
An angle measures rotation between two rays that share a vertex. A full turn is 360°, a half turn is 180°, and a quarter turn is 90°. Degree measure is not a length: two arcs can have different lengths while subtending the same angle if their radii differ. This distinction becomes essential when degrees are used to describe positions on Earth.

Angles may be measured clockwise or counterclockwise from a reference direction. In standard coordinate geometry, angles are commonly measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. A bearing uses a different convention: it is measured clockwise from north and written with three digits, such as 045° or 270°. Converting between conventions requires identifying the reference ray before doing arithmetic.

Compass directions provide useful benchmarks. North is 000° (or 360°), east is 090°, south is 180°, and west is 270°. A bearing of 135° points southeast because it lies halfway between east and south. The opposite, or reciprocal, bearing differs by 180° after wrapping the result into the interval from 000° to 359°.

Angular separation is the smaller rotation between two directions unless a problem explicitly asks for signed rotation. For bearings a and b, compute |a − b|. If that difference exceeds 180°, subtract it from 360°. Thus the smaller separation between 350° and 020° is 30°, not 330°.

Degrees can be divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds. The notation 42° 30′ 00″ is 42.5° because 30/60 = 0.5. Decimal degrees are easier to calculate with, while degrees–minutes–seconds remain common in navigation and surveying. Always label which representation you are using.

The central habit is to separate three questions: What is the reference direction? Which way is rotation measured? Do we want signed rotation or the smaller angular separation? Once those are explicit, bearings and geographic coordinates become ordinary, checkable geometry.

skills.name: Circles, arcs, and angular distance
skills.description: Relate central angles to arc length and use radians or degree fractions to measure distance along a circle.
skills.theory:
A central angle has its vertex at the centre of a circle. It intercepts an arc, and the arc’s share of the circumference is the same as the angle’s share of a full turn. In degrees, s = (θ/360°)·2πr, where s is arc length, θ is the central angle, and r is radius.

Radians express the same relationship more directly. One radian is the angle that intercepts an arc equal in length to the radius. Because a full circumference is 2πr, a full turn is 2π radians. When θ is in radians, arc length is s = rθ. Never place a degree value directly into s = rθ without converting it.

Conversion follows from 180° = π radians. Multiply degrees by π/180 to obtain radians, and multiply radians by 180/π to obtain degrees. Familiar benchmarks are 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, and 180° = π.

Angular distance and linear distance answer different questions. Two points separated by 10° on a small circle are closer together than two points separated by 10° on a large circle. On a sphere, the same angular separation also represents different east–west distances at different latitudes because circles of latitude shrink toward the poles.

The shortest route constrained to the circumference of a circle is the minor arc when the central angle is at most 180°. On a sphere the analogue is a segment of a great circle—a circle whose centre is the sphere’s centre. This is why long-distance routes can look curved on common flat maps while still following the shortest surface path.

Estimation is a useful safeguard. A 90° arc must be one quarter of a circumference; a 1° arc must be 1/360. If a calculation violates that scale, check units and whether the angle was converted correctly.

skills.name: Spherical coordinates and great-circle models
skills.description: Extend coordinate reasoning from a plane to a sphere and model angular separation, meridians, parallels, and great-circle distance.
skills.theory:
A flat coordinate plane uses perpendicular x- and y-axes. A sphere has no single flat grid that covers its surface without distortion, so positions are described by angles. Geographic latitude measures angular displacement north or south of the equatorial plane. Longitude measures angular displacement east or west around Earth from a chosen prime meridian.

Parallels are circles of constant latitude. The equator is the largest parallel and a great circle. Other parallels are smaller circles because their planes do not pass through Earth’s centre. Meridians are halves of great circles joining the poles. Opposite meridians together form a complete great circle.

Latitude ranges from 90° south to 90° north. Longitude is commonly represented from 180° west to 180° east, or equivalently from 0° to 360°. These conventions create wrap-around: 179°E and 179°W are only 2° apart across the antimeridian, not 358° apart.

North–south distance is comparatively simple in a spherical model because one degree of latitude always spans the same central angle on a meridian. East–west distance per degree of longitude shrinks with latitude. At latitude φ, the radius of the parallel is approximately R cos φ, so one degree of longitude spans about (πR/180) cos φ.

For general pairs of points, their longitude and latitude differences do not form an ordinary Cartesian right triangle over large distances. A great-circle calculation accounts for spherical geometry. The haversine formula is numerically stable: a = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ sin²(Δλ/2), c = 2 atan2(√a, √(1−a)), and distance d = Rc. Angles must be in radians.

Earth is not a perfect sphere. Precise surveying uses an ellipsoid and an explicit geodetic datum. A spherical calculation is a model whose adequacy depends on purpose: excellent for conceptual and many regional estimates, insufficient for boundary surveying or high-precision navigation.

The essential bridge is conceptual. Latitude and longitude are not arbitrary labels placed on a flat map; they are angular coordinates on a curved surface. Any flat display is a projection of that geometry and therefore introduces structured distortion.
